body.p: G
GAAL

Eved’s/Ebed’s son, who persuaded the men of Shekem/Shechem to revolt against Avimelek/Abimelech, the judge of Yisrael/Israel. The revolt, however, was quickly crushed and Shekem was destroyed (Jgs 9:26-41).
GAASH

1. Mountain about 20 miles (32.2 kilometers) southwest of Shekem/Shechem. Yehoshua/Joshua was buried at Timnat-Serah/Timnath-serah (Timnat-Heres/Timnath-heres) in the hill country of Efrayim/Ephraim, near Mt Ga’ash/Gaash (Jos 24:30; Jgs 2:9).
2. Stream in the vicinity of the mountain, mentioned as the home of Hiday/Hiddai (alternately Huray/Hurai), one of King David’s mighty soldiers (2 Sm 23:30; 1 Chr 11:32).
GABA*
KJV spelling of the Benyamite/Benjamite city, Geva/Geba, in Joshua 18:24, Ezra 2:26, and Nehemiah 7:30. See Geba.
GABAEL
1. Ancestor of Tovi/Tobit and a member of the tribe of Naftali/Naphtali (Tb 1:1).

2. Brother or son of Gabrias and resident of Rages, a city in Media, with whom Tovi left in trust 10 talents of silver (Tb 1:14). Tovi later told his son Toviyah/Tobias about the money, and Toviyah was led by the angel Refael/Raphael to Gabael (4:1, 20; 5:6; 6:9; 10:2).
GABATHA*
Alternate name for Bigtan/Bigthan, one of Ahashverosh’s/Ahasuerus’ eunuchs (Add Est 12:1). See Bigthan, Bigthana.
GABBAI
Head of a family that returned to Yerushalem/Jerusalem with Zerubavel/Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile (Neh 11:8).
GABBATHA

Transliteration of an uncertain Aramaic expression, which is rendered in Greek as “paved with stones” and refers to the raised area before the palace in Yerushalem/Jerusalem where formal sentencing by the governor occurred. Pilatos/Pilate seated himself on the elevated judgment seat here in order to preside over the trial of Yeshua/Jesus (Jn 19:13).
GABRI, GABRIAS*
Brother or father of Gabael. The genitive case of the original does not make the exact relationship certain; it simply specifies that there is a relationship (Tb 1:14; 4:20).
See also Gabael #2.
GABRIEL

One of the two angels mentioned by name in the Bible (the other is Mika’el/Michael). Gavriel/Gabriel appeared in human form to Daniyel/Daniel to reveal to him the meaning of a vision, to show what would transpire on the Day of Judgment, and to give Daniyel wisdom and understanding (Dn 8:16; 9:21-22). In the NT Gavriel appeared to Zekaryah/Zechariah the priest as he served in the temple, to announce the birth of Zekaryah’s son, Yohan/John the immerser (Lk 1:11-20). Six months later Gavriel appeared to Maria/Mary to announce that she would become the mother of Yeshua/Jesus, the long-awaited Messiah (Lk 1:26-33). Gavriel is commonly called an archangel but is not referred to as such in the Bible.

There is an abundance of material about Gavriel in the noncanonical writings of the Yehudim/Jews. In the books of Hanok/Enoch he is pictured as one of the four chief angels, along with Mika’el, Refael/Raphael, and Uriel (1 Enoch 40:3, 6). He is one of the holy angels (20:7) who looks down from heaven and is a principal intercessor (1 Enoch 9:1; 40:6; 2 Enoch 21:3). He is to destroy the wicked (1 Enoch 9:9-10) and cast them into the furnace (54:6) and is set over all powers (40:9). Mika’el sits at God’s right hand, and Gavriel sits on the left (2 Enoch 24:1). Mika’el, as guardian angel of Yisrael/Israel (cf. Dn 12:1) and a high priest of heaven, is more occupied with affairs in heaven, but Gavriel is God’s messenger who goes from heaven to execute God’s will on earth.
See also Angel.
GAD (Person)

1. One of the 12 sons of Ya’akov/Jacob (Gn 35:26; 1 Chr 2:2). He was the first of the two sons born to Ya’akov by Zilpah, Le’ah’s/Leah’s maid. Delighted with giving Ya’akov another son, Le’ah named the boy Gad, meaning “good fortune” (Gn 30:11). Later, Gad moved his family with Ya’akov to Mitsrayim/Egypt (Ex 1:4). When Ya’akov blessed his sons, he predicted that Gad would constantly be troubled by foreign invaders but would successfully withstand them and put them to flight (see Gn 49:19 and discussion below under Gad, Tribe of). Gad became the father of seven sons (Gn 46:16) and the founder of the Gadim/Gadites (Dt 3:12, 16), one of the 12 tribes of Yisrael/Israel (Nm 2:14).
See also Gad, Tribe of.

2. Prophet and seer during the reign of David. He counseled David to leave Mitspah/Mizpeh of Moav/Moab and return to the land of Yehudah/Judah (1 Sm 22:5). Gad communicated David’s punishment for numbering the fighting men of Yisrael (2 Sm 24:11-14, 18-19; 1 Chr 21:9-19), assisted David and Natan/Nathan in setting up the order of worship in the sanctuary (2 Chr 29:25) and later wrote an account of David’s life (1 Chr 29:29).
GAD* (Idol)
Kena’ani/Canaanite god of fortune or fate whom the Israelis/Israelites worshiped (Is 65:11).
See also Canaanite Deities and Religion.
GAD, Tribe of

Descendants of Ya’akov’s/Jacob’s seventh son Gad (Gn 30:11; Nm 1:24-25), and eighth largest of the 12 tribes that came out of Mitsrayim/Egypt with Mosheh/Moses (according to the number of warriors in Nm 1:1-3, 24-25). They raised livestock and had a reputation for being fierce in battle (Nm 32:1; Dt 33:20).

During the wilderness period, they were led by Elyasaf’s/Eliasaph’s son Deuel (Nm 1:14; 2:14; 7:42; 10:20). When Yisrael/Israel encamped, Gad was located south of the tabernacle behind the tribes of Re’uven/Reuben and Shim’on/Simeon (2:14-15). They are mentioned at the tribal offering to the tabernacle, and after the plague, which God brought upon Yisrael (7:42-47; 26:15, 18). Maki’s son Geuel represented the tribe as one of the 12 spies sent by Mosheh into Kena’an/Canaan (13:15).

At the close of the wilderness period, Gad, Re’uven, and half of Menasheh’s/Manasseh’s tribe requested permission to settle east of the Yarden/Jordan, for it had good pastureland (Nm 32:1-2). This was permitted on the condition that they would help in the conquest of Kena’an (Nm 32:20-22; Jos 1:12-18).

During the Conquest under Yehoshua/Joshua, Gad is mentioned only at the battle of Yeriho/Jericho (Jos 4:12). After the end of the conflict, Gad, Re’uven, and half of Menasheh settled their land east of the Yarden (cf. Nm 34:13-14; Jos 12:6; 13:8).

Gad’s inheritance was between Menasheh’s tribe to the north and Re’uven’s to the south. The Aravi/Arabian Desert formed its eastern border and the Yarden River its western. There seem to have been no fixed borders between the two and a half tribes, and the whole area was often referred to as Gilead and Bashan (2 Kgs 10:33). Its land ran north to the Sea of Kineret/Chinnereth (Galil/Galilee), but among the mountains it seems to have run eastward only as far as the Yabok/Jabbok River. To the south, the cities of Aroer and Heshbon mark their southern limits (Dt 3:12-13; Jos 12:1-6; 13:24-28).

The history of Gad from its settlement to the Captivity was closely tied with the two neighboring Hebrew tribes. Shortly after returning to their lands, these two and a half tribes almost started a civil war by erecting a large altar (Jos 22:10-34). During the time of the judges, Gilead (including Gad) was threatened, if not occupied, by the Amonim/Ammonites until they were defeated by Yiftah/Jephthah (Jgs 11). Some Gadim/Gadites joined David at Tsiklag/Ziklag during his exile (1 Chr 12:14, 37). In the 14th year of David’s reign the two and a half tribes were formally brought together under an overseer named Yeriyah/Jerijah (and his brothers, 26:30-32).

During the time of the divided kingdom, the tribes east of the Yarden were constantly under attack. During Yehu’s/Jehu’s reign (841–814 BC), Hazael annexed all the land east of the Yarden, and they were later carried off into captivity by Tiglat-Pileser/Tiglath-pileser, king of Ashur/Assyria (2 Kgs 15:29; 1 Chr 5:26-27). Subsequently, the Amonim occupied Gad’s land (Jer 49:1).

In the postexilic period Gad is mentioned only once—in Yehezkel’s/Ezekiel’s vision of the restoration of Yisrael (Ez 48:1, 27-28, 34). In the NT, Gad is mentioned only in the book of Revelation, in the list of the tribes sealed by God (Rv 7:5).
See also Israel, History of; Gad (Person) #1.
GAD*, Valley of

Translation of a Hebrew phrase in 2 Samuel 24:5, meaning literally “the river or streambed of Gad.” It is rendered “in the midst of the river of Gad” (kjv), “in the middle of the valley, toward Gad” (rsv), “the valley of Gad” (asv) and “in the direction of Gad” (nlt). The valley of Gad was the beginning point for David’s census, and the “river” or “valley” is undoubtedly the Arnon.
GADARA*, GADARENES

City of the Dekapolis/Decapolis and its inhabitants, mentioned only once in the better manuscripts of the NT. Yeshua/Jesus had crossed to the eastern side of the Sea of Galil/Galilee and healed the demoniac named Legion, whom he encountered in “the country of the Gadarainos/Gadarenes” (Mt 8:28). Markos’s/Mark’s account in 5:1 and Lukas’s/Luke’s in 8:26, 37 read “Gerasainon/Gerasenes.” (The kjv, following the Textus Receptus, has variant names here; in Matthew 8:28 it reads “Gergesenes,” and in Markos and Lukas it reads “Gadarainos.”) The variant names among the Gospel writers may be due to the fact that Gerasa was the wider geographical area of which Gadara was a chief city. Geographers conclude that the most likely location for the leap of the swine into the sea would have been a strip of steep coastline near Gergesa, a smaller, less important town of the area. This would fit another suggestion that Matay/Matthew was a native of the region and so he pinpointed the precise place, while Markos and Lukas intended to point out the general location for their Greek and Roman readers, since Gergesa was small and relatively unknown, while Gadara was a Greek city of some importance.

The name Gadara indicates that the city was of Semitic origin. It was located five to six miles (8 to 10 kilometers) southeast of the Sea of Galil, and its territory included the hot springs of el Hamme, north of the Yarmuk River. The first reference to it in history was when it was captured by Antiokos/Antiochus III (218 BC). Later, it was taken by the Yehudim/Jews under Alexandros/Alexander Janneus (103 BC), and the inhabitants were enslaved and forced to receive the law of Mosheh/Moses. The city was demolished by the Yehudim, but when the area was reconquered by Pompey, it was rebuilt (63 BC). It became a free city under Pompey and joined the federation of Greek cities in the Transjordan known as the Dekapolis. Augustus Kaisar/Caesar added Gadara to the territory of Herodes/Herod the Great (30 BC), and at Herodes’s death it was annexed to Aram/Syria (4 BC). During the Jewish rebellion (AD 66–70), Vespasian took the city, and it continued to flourish for many years. It was the seat of a Christian bishopric from AD 325 until the Muslim conquest. See Decapolis; Gerasa, Gerasenes; Gergesa, Gergesenes.
GADDI
Man from Menasheh’s/Manasseh’s tribe sent by Mosheh/Moses to search out the land of Kena’an/Canaan (Nm 13:11).
GADDIEL
Sodi’s son from Zevulun’s/Zebulun’s tribe, sent by Mosheh/Moses to search out the land of Kena’an/Canaan (Nm 13:10).
GADFLY

Any of a number of large flies, including the horsefly and botfly, that irritate livestock. King Nevukadnetsar/Nebuchadnezzar is called a gadfly in the only biblical reference to this insect (Jer 46:20). See Animals (Fly).
GADI
Father of Menahem. Menahem revolted and killed Shalum/Shallum, king of Yisrael/Israel, placing himself on the throne as king (2 Kgs 15:14, 17).
GADITE
Member of Gad’s tribe (Dt 3:12, 16). See Gad (Person) #1; Gad, Tribe of.
GAHAM
Son of Nahor, Avraham’s/Abraham’s brother, and his concubine Re’umah/Reumah (Gn 22:24).
GAHAR
Ancestor of a group of temple assistants that returned to Yerushalem/Jerusalem with Zerubavel/Zerubbabel after the exile (Ezr 2:47; Neh 7:49).
GAIUS

1. Native of Makedonia/Macedonia and traveling companion of Paulos/Paul during the apostle’s third missionary journey. He and Aristarkos/Aristarchus were both seized at Efesos/Ephesus during the riot caused by Demetrios/Demetrius the silversmith (Acts 19:29).
2. Native of Derbai/Derbe in Lukaonia/Lycaonia, who traveled with Paulos from Efesos to Makedonia (Acts 20:4). Some have identified him with #1 above.

3. Prominent believer in Korinthos/Corinth and host to Paulos and the whole church there (Rom 16:23). Since Romans was written in Korinthos, the Gaios/Gaius mentioned in 1 Corinthians 1:14 was probably the same person. If so, he was baptized by Paulos.
4. Man to whom Yohan/John addressed his third letter (3 Jn 1:1).
GALAL
1. Levite and Mica’s son, who returned from exile in Bavel/Babylon (1 Chr 9:15).
2. Levite and forefather of Ovadyah/Obadiah (Avda/Abda). Ovadyah returned from exile in Bavel (1 Chr 9:16; Neh 11:17).
GALATIA

Ancient kingdom resulting from migrations of Gallic people from the west and settlement on the central plain of Asia Minor. An earlier migratory movement resulted in the sack of Romai/Rome by the Gauls (or Celts) in 390 BC, but in a later attempt to overrun Yavan/Greece the Gallic invaders were repulsed. That unsuccessful invasion into Yavan led the Gauls to turn their attention to Asia Minor. They penetrated the larger part of the area but were defeated by Atalos/Attalus I in 230 BC. As a result, they became restricted to that part of Asia later known as Galatia. By that time, the Gauls consisted of three tribes, the Trocmi, Tolistobogii, and Tectosages, which settled into the towns of Tavium, Pessinus, and Ancyra, respectively. In 189 BC these Galatians were subdued by the Romans but were allowed to govern themselves.

After the death of Amyntas in 25 BC, Galatia became a Roman province. Within its boundaries were the ethnic areas of Galatia proper, Lukaonia/Lycaonia, Isauria, and parts of Frugia/Phrygia and Pisidia. The new province, therefore, included the towns of Derbai/Derbe, Lustra/Lystra, Ikonion/Iconium, and Pisidian Antiokeia/Antioch, all of which the apostle Paulos/Paul visited on his first missionary journey. The term “Galatia” was used in two different ways, one to describe the area occupied by the Gauls in the north, and the other to describe the whole Roman province, including the southern towns. That ambiguity has given rise to a problem over the destination of Paulos’s letter to the Galatians.

The original inhabitants of north Galatia were Phrygians, many of whom still remained in the first century AD, together with some Greeks and a fairly large community of Yehudim/Jews. Although the area was cosmopolitan, the Celtic element predominated. These people were known for their sturdy independence as well as for their drunkenness and revelings. In religious matters there is evidence that they were highly superstitious and were especially attracted to the wild rites of the goddess Cybele.

In towns of the southern region, Greek influence was more pronounced, especially among the more educated members of the communities. But the Phrygian element was still strong among the humbler inhabitants. They, too, were predominately devotees of Cybele, although there the cult had become modified by Greek influences. In Pisidian Antiokeia, for instance, the goddess was known as the Genius of Antiokeia, while in Ikonion she was known as Athena Polias.

Geographically the northern towns, situated on a well-watered plateau and served by a major road from the Aegean shores to the west, became prosperous centers of commerce. But access from north to south was difficult and communication poor because of the mountainous terrain leading up to the plateau. The southern towns were situated on the route between Aram/Syria and Asia. Their strategic location explains why churches were established in those towns on Paulos’s first missionary journey (cf. Acts 13–14).

Galatia, linked with Frugia, is mentioned in Acts 16:6 and 18:23, but it is not clear whether Paulos ever visited or established churches in the northern area. The only other references to Galatia in the NT are probably to the southern towns (1 Cor 16:1; 2 Tm 4:10; 1 Pt 1:1). See Galatians, Letter to the.
GALATIANS, Letter to the
This letter has an important place in the NT. It reveals much of Paulos’s/Paul’s character and sheds light on his teaching. It has appropriately been called the charter of Christian liberty.

Author

The author of the epistle is explicitly stated to be Paulos the apostle (Gal 1:1). The letter gives some brief but telling glimpses of his experience before he became a Christian. He mentions his former life in Youdaismos/Judaism (v 13). The fact that he had been a thoroughly devout Yehudi/Jew has an important bearing on what he writes in this letter. He remembered his passionate devotion to his former faith, in whose cause he had violently persecuted the church of God. He reminded the Galatians about this, for the Jewish traditions had meant a great deal to him. There is no doubt that he had once regarded his violent opposition to the church as a religious act of the highest order. Indeed, his strong devotion to Youdaismos sets in clear relief the remarkable transformation that occurred when he became a Christian. A revelation from God, he was convinced, gave him special authority to write the way he did.

In this epistle he mentioned two features of his conversion experience that had a profound effect on him. One is the purpose of God for his life, which he recognized as reaching back even before he was born (v 15). He did not go into detail, but he never tired of talking about the grace of God. He had turned his back on the idea of earning merit through his own efforts. The second aspect of his conversion that deeply impressed him was the recognition that his call to preach could be traced to that occasion. When he preached to the Galatians, he did so with divine authority because he was conscious of having received a divine commission. The apostles and elders of the church did not decide it would be a good thing for him to preach the gospel; it was God who planned it. Moreover, Paulos was equally convinced that the gospel he preached was not of his own making. He had received it through a revelation of Yeshua/Jesus Christ (v 12).

Paulos went to some lengths to demonstrate that he had received his apostleship from God (1:1). He was conscious not only of a call to preach but also of a call to exercise apostolic authority on an equal footing with the Yerushalem/Jerusalem apostles. He certainly seemed to be on the defensive, but this was prompted by the special situation that had arisen among the Galatians and that caused this letter to be written.

Paulos gives one biographical detail in this letter that is not mentioned in his other letters. He states that after his conversion he went away into Arav/Arabia (1:17). The apostle does not tell us what he did there, but probably he was quietly reorienting his thoughts. According to the book of Acts, when he returned to Damesek/Damascus he powerfully proved that Yeshua was the Messiah (Acts 9:22). He also refers to traveling in Aram/Syria and Kilikia/Cilicia (Gal 1:21), which must have been prior to his first missionary journey.
Destination and Date
It is impossible to determine the date of this letter before discussing its destination.
Destination

Paulos/Paul addresses his letter to the Galatians. But there has been much debate over where they lived, because the term Galatia was used in two different senses. It was used of the province that stretched from the borders of Pamfulia/Pamphylia in the southern part of Asia Minor to the border of Pontos/Pontus toward the northern seacoast. The term was also used of a part of the province in the north where a group of people from Gaul had settled and given their name to the whole area. Hence “Galatia” could mean either the geographical area in the north or the whole province. It is not easy to decide what the term meant when used by Paulos. The debate is between the view that the term was used geographically, in which case some churches in the north are in mind (North Galatikos/Galatian Theory), or politically, in which case Paulos may be referring to the churches in southern Galatia founded on his first missionary journey (South Galatikos Theory). It may at first sight seem a quite unimportant issue, but since the decision affects the date of the letter and to some extent its occasion and purpose, a review of the positions must be made.

Until the beginning of the 20th century, no one seems to have questioned that Paulos was writing to the inhabitants of the geographical district in the northern part of the province. This view agrees with the oldest use of the term, since the provinces did not come into existence until 25 BC, whereas there were Galatians in the north some time before this. It is reasonable to suppose that the southerners would not have taken too kindly to being addressed as “Galatians.” It may be argued that most people in those days would have thought of the northern peoples when hearing the name.

Lukas’s/Luke’s habit when writing Acts was to use geographical rather than political descriptions of places. He refers, for instance, to Lustra/Lystra and Derbai/Derbe as cities of Lukaonia/Lycaonia, not as cities of Galatia. It is reasonable, therefore, that when he refers to Frugia/Phrygia and Galatia in Acts 16:6 and 18:23, he means that Paulos went through the northern area. There were three main towns in that district—Ancyra, Tavium, and Pessinus—and it would therefore follow that Paulos must have established churches there.

The traditional North Galatikos view has, however, been challenged. It is pointed out that although Lukas prefers geographical descriptions, Paulos prefers political ones for grouping his churches. In this letter he mentions the churches of Christ in Judea (1:22). Elsewhere he mentions the “churches of Asia” (1 Cor 16:19). Several times Paulos refers to the believers in Makedonia/Macedonia (e.g., 2 Cor 8:1; 9:2; 1 Thes 4:10) and in Akaia/Achaia (1 Cor 16:15; 2 Cor 1:1), while both are mentioned together in Romans 15:26, 2 Corinthians 9:2, and 1 Thessalonians 1:7. This seems to be Paulos’s normal habit, in which case a letter addressed to the Galatians would be circulated to all the existing churches in the province of Galatia.

South Galatikos supporters do not agree that the southern people would have resented the name Galatians, maintaining that there would have been no other name available with which to describe them. One fairly positive piece of evidence is found in Paulos’s statement that it was because of a bodily ailment that he first preached to the Galatians (Gal 4:13). But a glance at the map, particularly a relief map, would show that the route to the northern area was over mountainous terrain, and it is difficult to think that a sick man would have attempted it. Under the southern theory, the journey would have been much shorter and less arduous.

Another argument in support of the South Galatikos Theory assumes that Acts 20:4, which mentions the names of those who accompanied Paulos to Yerushalem, is referring to delegates appointed by the churches in support of the collection to aid the poor churches of Judea. If this assumption is right, it is noticeable that no representative is included from the northern area, although both Gaios/Gaius and Timotheos/Timothy were from the south. This would be more weighty if Acts had actually mentioned the collection. One last point is that Barnabas is mentioned three times (Gal 2:1, 9, 13) suggesting that he is known to the readers. Yet according to Acts, he accompanied Paulos only on the first missionary journey.
It is difficult to reach a conclusion, but it seems that the arguments for a South Galatikos Theory have more weight than those for the older theory.
Date

Under the North Galatikos Theory, it is claimed that the letter was written after the events mentioned in Acts 18:23—that is, during the course of the third missionary journey (c. AD 56), possibly while Paulos was at Efesos/Ephesus or soon after.

On the other hand, if the letter was addressed to the south Galatikos churches founded on the first missionary journey, any date after that journey is possible, including during the third journey, as mentioned above. But a further possibility opens up since a much earlier date might more readily fit into the background of the letter. Thus, it is possible that this letter is among the earliest that Paulos wrote.

The main problem with assigning a date is that in Galatians 1–2 Paulos mentions two visits to Yerushalem/Jerusalem (1:18; 2:1), whereas Acts mentions (or implies) three visits (Acts 9:26; 11:29-30; 15:2). It has traditionally been supposed that the second visit (2:1) can be identified with the events of Acts 15. This would mean that Paulos was giving his own account of the decisions of the so-called Council of Yerushalem. There is much to be said for this view. There are similarities between the two passages. In both, Barnabas is mentioned. In both, questions are asked about the circumcision of the Gentiles. And in both, Paulos and Barnabas give a report about the matter to the Yerushalem leaders. The main difficulty is that Paulos’s wording in Galatians 2:1 suggests that this event took place on his second visit to Yerushalem, whereas Acts 15 relates his third visit. It is traditionally explained that on the second visit Paulos and Barnabas had no contact with the apostles but simply handed over the collection from the Antiokeia/Antioch church to the Yerushalem elders (cf. Acts 11:30). A difficulty with this view is that Galatians 2 speaks only of conversations with the three leading apostles at Yerushalem and does not mention the whole church (as Acts 15 clearly does). Paulos does not refer to the decision reached by the church, but only to his agreement with those he calls the “pillar” apostles. It could, of course, be that before the general meeting of Acts 15 (which occured in AD 50), Paulos and Barnabas had a behind-the-scenes meeting with the leaders and preferred to mention the decision reached with them rather than quote an ecclesiastical edict. This may also explain another difficulty—the lack of any mention of the prohibitions that the Yerushalem church imposed on the Gentiles (Acts 15:20). Paulos simply mentions the need to remember the poor (Gal 2:10). Yet another difficulty with the traditional view is that Paulos mentions his dispute with Kefa/Peter over the question of Gentile-Jewish fellowship (vv 11-14) after his account of the agreement reached with the Yerushalem apostles. This places Kefa in a compromising position. It is difficult to explain his inconsistency. He may have agreed that Gentiles should not be circumcised, but then vacillated over the question of fellowship.

An alternative view suggests that when Paulos/Paul and Barnabas went to Yerushalem with the collection they also had private talks with the leading apostles. Acts 11:29-30 is set in a period of political activity against the apostles (Acts 12 records the martyrdom of Ya’akov/James and the arrest of Kefa), and this may explain the private nature of the meeting. This interpretation would explain why Paulos makes no mention of the church’s decision—because the meeting happened before the Yerushalem Council. It would also make it easier to explain Kefa’s actions at Antiokeia, if this behavior occurred before the church as a whole had discussed and resolved the matter. According to this view, Paulos’s Letter to the Galatians may be the earliest of his letters (pre–AD 50).

There are, however, some difficulties with this view. Acts 11:30 mentions no apostles as meeting Paulos and Barnabas. Nor is there any reference to Titos/Titus, whom Paulos says they took with them (Gal 2:1). Further, Paulos’s references to preaching among the Gentiles (v 2) would seem to require a date after the first missionary journey, unless he was thinking of his work in Antiokeia, a Jewish-Gentile church.

It is difficult to decide between these two views. Chronological considerations (based on Paulos’s mention of 14 years in 2:1) slightly favor a later date, while the relationship of the content of this epistle to the Yerushalem Council (AD 50) points to an early date.
Purpose and Theological Teaching

Difficulties had arisen in the Galatikos/Galatian churches because a group of people had been insisting that Gentiles must be circumcised. These people must have been Judaizers, that is, Christian Yehudim/Jews who could see no hope for Gentiles unless they accepted circumcision as an initiatory rite. Linked with this was a criticism of Paulos’s apostolic status. The opponents were claiming the support of the Yerushalem apostles, whom they regarded as superior to Paulos. This would explain why Paulos saw the issue so clearly as a challenge to the gospel he preached. His letter strongly expressed his understanding of the seriousness of the situation.

Interpretation will vary slightly according to which date one assigns to the letter. If it was written before the Yerushalem Council (Acts 15), the circumcision issue had not yet been thrashed out and the Galatikos situation would be the first major crisis over it. But if the Yerushalem Council had already happened, the south Galatikos churches would already have received those decisions (16:4), and apparently had allowed themselves to be affected by Judaizers who took a harder line than the Yerushalem apostles had. If the northern churches are indicated, there is no direct evidence to show that they had received the decrees.

We may conclude that the apostle’s aim in this letter is twofold—to maintain the validity of his apostleship, and to uphold the character of the gospel he preached. In the first part of the letter he is concerned to show his relationship with the Yerushalem “pillar” apostles in order to demonstrate his equality with them, while at the same time claiming his independence of them. Moreover, he asserts that there is only one gospel, which suggests that his opponents were charging him with preaching a different gospel. But he claims to have received his gospel from God, not from men.

In the course of his letter, Paulos expressed some important theological truths. The main body of the letter issues a strong warning against a form of legalism that is applicable not only to the situation Paulos confronted in the Galatikos churches but wherever dependence on legal observances is considered essential for salvation. If a Gentile could not become a Christian without being circumcised, it would not only make an external rite a condition for Christian salvation but in addition would imply a commitment to keep the whole Jewish law. When Paulos argued against justification by works of the law, he showed the superiority of justification by faith or lawkeeping. The whole letter extols the doctrine of grace.

Nevertheless, in contesting the doctrine of works, the apostle gave no support to spiritual license. He posited that the alternative to legalism is not the absence of all restraint. Although Christ has secured freedom for the believer, that freedom must not be used to indulge the flesh (Gal 5:13). Indeed, Paulos’s exposition of the Christian life in this letter is of a high moral order. He sets the standard himself by declaring that he has been crucified with Christ (2:20). Not only is this letter a charter for Christian liberty, but it is also a charter for Christian living.
Content
Introduction (1:1-5)

The opening to this letter is more abrupt than those in Paulos’s/Paul’s other letters. He omits the usual thanksgiving and expands the usual greeting. In the first words he strongly affirms the divine origin of his apostleship.
The Opponents (1:6-10)
Paulos is astonished that the Galatians have allowed themselves to be influenced so quickly by those who were perverting the gospel. He expresses an anathema against any who preach another gospel.
A Defense of His Apostleship (1:11–2:14)

There are several stages in Paulos’s argument about his own position. He states that his teaching has come from God, not from men, showing his awareness that God has not only called him to be an apostle but has also sanctioned his gospel. It is important for him to make clear that he is not dependent on others for his position, although he proceeds to show that there is no difference between him and the leading apostles (1:11-12). He next contrasts his former zeal in Youdaismos/Judaism with his calling to preach the gospel, again emphasizing the divine nature of his call (vv 13-17).

He then proceeds to mention that he has on two occasions had meetings with the Yerushalem/Jerusalem apostles. As a result, he has been offered the right hand of fellowship—a way of showing that there is no disagreement between them. It was agreed that Paulos should be entrusted with the gospel for the uncircumcised, and that Kefa/Peter should go to the circumcised. There was no questioning of Paulos’s apostleship. They all agreed on the Christian responsibility to remember the poor (1:18–2:10).

In order to give a tangible example of his apostolic position, Paulos mentions the occasion of his public rebuke of Kefa. Kefa had acted inconsistently for fear of certain men who had come from Ya’akov/James in Yerushalem, and who were representatives of the circumcision party. Paulos’s challenge to Kefa sets the scene for the introduction of the doctrinal part of the letter (2:11-14).
A Defense of the Gospel (2:15–4:31)
Paulos introduces the issue of justification by works of the law and contrasts it with justification by faith. He sees the whole situation as a choice between Christ and the law (2:15-21).

His aim is to show the superiority of Christianity over Youdaismos in the matter of salvation. He notes first that the Galatians had become Christians through the Spirit and wonders what is possessing them to return to the works of the law, which Paulos then equates with the “flesh” (3:1-5).

Avraham/Abraham is brought into the discussion presumably because the opponents were maintaining that only Avraham’s seed would receive the inheritance, and circumcision was regarded as an indispensable sign of a son of the covenant. But Paulos points out that even Avraham was justified by faith, not by the law (3:6-9).

Indeed, the law could only bring a curse on those who disobeyed. This leads Paulos/Paul to show how Christ has become a curse for us. Hence, he claims that in Christ we may still inherit the blessing promised to Avraham (3:10-14).

Paulos anticipates that some may say it is invalid to appeal to the promise to Avraham to counteract justification by works of the law. He shows that the promise preceded the law by four centuries and cannot be invalidated by it (3:15-18).

This leads the apostle to reflect on the function of the law. He points out that it served to prepare the way for Christ by showing mankind’s need and by revealing its own inability to give life. Paulos calls the law our custodian, whose function (in ancient times) was to guard and guide a son until he reached the age of independence (3:19-29).

The contrast between those under a guardian versus fully independent sons causes Paulos to reflect on the superior position of sons. The Spirit of God has enabled believers to call God “Abba” (Father), something the law could not do (4:1-7).

The apostle has made his point, but he supports it with a personal appeal. He reminds his readers of their state of bondage before they became Christians and deplores that they have returned to such a state in wanting to observe ritual feast days after the Jewish manner. He also reminds them of the former affectionate relationship they had with him when they first became Christians. He is deeply affected by their present attitude (4:8-20). Finally, Paulos appeals to a scriptural allegory in support of his argument. He sees Yitshak/Isaac and Yishmael/Ishmael, both sons of Avraham, as representing the distinction between sonship and slavery, which he has already mentioned (vv 21-31).
Practical Advice (5:1–6:10)

Paulos proceeds to draw out the practical consequences of his doctrinal arguments. He sets out the way in which those who are liberated in Christ should live. They should not commit themselves to Youdaismos/Judaism by submitting to circumcision (5:1-6). Paulos again attacks those who were leading the Galatians astray (vv 7-12). The new principle that must replace legalism is love. Love is possible only by living in the Spirit. This will lead not only to a rejection of the works of the flesh but also to the development of the fruit of the Spirit (5:13-26). The spiritual man will have a concern for the burdened and will seek to help others, particularly fellow Christians (6:1-10).
Conclusion (6:11-18)

Paulos now takes the pen and writes his final word with his own hand. He sees fit to contrast his own aim in glorying in the cross of Christ with his opponents’ aim to glory in the flesh. There are no greetings at the end of this letter, only a request that no one should bother him further.
See also Galatia; Judaizers; Law, Biblical Concept of; Paul, The Apostle.
GALBANUM

One of the ingredients used to make a special perfume for the tabernacle (Ex 30:34). Galbanum comes from a waxy, brownish gum excreted from the lower part of a plant that is a member of the carrot or parsley family and is native to Aram/Syria and Paras/Persia. It is a tall herb that bears small, greenish-white flowers and fruit at the stem tip in bunches or clusters. Its leaves are compound and divided into many fine parts like the leaves of parsley or carrots. An incision made in the stem a few inches above soil level yields a milky sap that hardens. Galbanum is presently used in the manufacture of varnish.

Galbanum is mentioned in the apocryphal book of Ecclesiasticus as having a pleasant odor (24:15). Although galbanum is not an agreeable perfume when used alone, it was evidently mixed with other substances to yield a fragrant ointment.
See also Plants.
GALEED

Name meaning literally “a heap of witness.” Ya’akov/Jacob gave this name to a pile of stones erected as a witness to the pact of friendship made between himself and his father-in-law, Lavan/Laban, who named the cairn Yegar-Sahaduta/Jegar-sahadutha (Gn 31:47-48). Its location is unknown. The name Gal’ed/Galeed is not to be confused with the name Gilead, designation of the territory east of the Yarden/Jordan.
GALILEE

Area in northern Palestine that, in Yisrael’s/Israel’s earlier history, had boundaries that were not clearly defined but that became more precisely defined in the period of Roman rule. The English name Galil/Galilee comes from two Hebrew words meaning “circuit” or “district.”
Historical Background

In OT times Galil was not significant in Israeli/Israelite life, but in NT times it was a prominent Jewish population center. Galil is first mentioned in the Bible as the location of Kedesh, a city of refuge in the hill country of Naftali/Naphtali (Jos 20:7; cf. 21:32; 1 Chr 6:76).

Galil originally designated the area occupied by the tribes of Naftali, Zevulun/Zebulun (Is 9:1), and possibly Asher (if Kavul/Cabul in Jos 19:27 is the same city as in 1 Kgs 9:11-13). None of those tribes was able to completely expel the original Kena’ani/Canaanite inhabitants (Jgs 1:30-33; 2:1-4), and as a result, Galil tended to be racially mixed. The cities that King Shelomoh/Solomon gave to Hiram, gentile king of Tsor/Tyre, were within Galil (1 Kgs 9:11), and the gentile intermixture in that area may have influenced Shelomoh’s choice of those cities for a gift. This racially mixed condition is also the probable basis for the designation in Isaiah 9:1, “Galil of the nations” (cf. Mt 4:15; 1 Macc 5:15).

During the monarchy, Galil was a buffer zone between Yisrael and Aram/Syria, and it bore the brunt of Arami/Syrian invasions against Yisrael. This fact is cited by the prophet Yeshayah/Isaiah (Is 9:1), but he saw it as the prelude to a brighter day when the messianic king would reign. Galil was conquered by Arami King Ben-Hadad/Ben-hadad (1 Kgs 15:20) and was probably recovered by Yisrael’s King Ahav/Ahab. Galil was later subjugated by the Arameans under Hazael (2 Kgs 10:32; 12:18; 13:22) and regained by Yarov’am/Jeroboam II (2 Kgs 14:23-25). As a result of Assyrian conquests in the area of Damesek/Damascus and Galil in 732 BC by Tiglat-Pileser/Tiglath-pileser III (2 Kgs 15:29), more Gentiles were imported into the area while many of the Jewish inhabitants were deported. This naturally led to greater gentile influence and domination in Galil. Under the successive influence of Bavel/Babylonia, Paras/Persia, Yavan/Greece, and Aram, Galil was constantly experiencing infiltration and migration. From the time of the Assyrian conquest of Yisrael to about the end of the second century BC, Galil’s population was dominated by Gentiles, with only a few Yehudim/Jews.

The Yehudim remaining in Galil were brought to Judea by Shim’on/Simon Maccabeus in 164 BC (1 Macc 5:21-23). Galil was conquered by Aristobulos/Aristobulus I (104–103 BC), who forced the inhabitants to be circumcised and to submit to Jewish laws, a work that probably already had been initiated by Yohan/John Hurkanos/Hyrcanus (134–104 BC).

Herodes/Herod the Great (ruler under Romai/Rome, 37–4 BC) affixed Galil to his kingdom, and more Yehudim were attracted there. Josephus recorded that Galil had 240 cities and villages and 100,000 men available to fight against the Romans. After the death of Herodes the Great, Galil was included in the tetrarchy of Herodes Antipas (4 BC–AD 39). With the banishment of Herodes Antipas in AD 39, Galil was added to the territory of Herodes Agrippas/Agrippa I, who ruled it until he died in AD 44. Romai directly administered Galil until it was put under the rule of Herodes Agrippas II. By siding with the Romans during the Jewish revolts, he was able to retain his position until AD 100. In spite of the Galilim’s/Galileans’ attempt to gain independence, the revolutionary faction was brought under subjection by Vespasian in AD 67. After Herodes Agrippas II’s death, Galil became part of the Roman province of Aram.

Following the fall of Yerushalem/Jerusalem in AD 70, the Sanhedrin and many other Yehudim of southern Palestine flocked to Galil. As a result, such cities as Tiberias and Sepphoris became Jewish, and the dispersed Yehudim came to think of Galil as their center. Tiberias became a center for Jewish learning, and it was there that such major contributions as the Tiberian system of vowel pointing the Hebrew consonantal text were made, as well as the formulation of the Mishnah and the Palestinian Talmud.

From about AD 451 until the Muslim rule over Galil began in the seventh century, Galil was governed by the Christian patriarchate of Yerushalem, set up by the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451. Muslim rule from the seventh century on was continuous except for the intervals caused by the twelfth-century Crusades and World War I. All of Galil has been included in the modern state of Yisrael since its establishment in 1948.
Boundaries

Galil/Galilee was bounded on the east by the upper Yarden/Jordan River and the Sea of Galil and on the south by the plain of Yizre’el/Esdraelon, which served as a natural boundary between Galil and Shomron/Samaria. At times the plain was included in Galil, as it was during the intertestamental period (1 Macc 10:30; 12:47-49). While the northern boundary was uncertain and variable during Galil’s history, in NT times it reached to Lake Huleh. The western boundary followed the Mediterranean Sea to Mt Karmel/Carmel.

From the time of the divided kingdom until the Assyrian conquest of Galil (734 BC), it was the northernmost part of the kingdom of Yisrael/Israel. The area was divided into upper Galil and lower Galil by the plain of Ramah, which ran between Kafarnaoum/Capernaum and Ptolemais (cf. Jdt 1:8; 1 Macc 12:49; Josephus’s War 3.3.1). In the Mishnah (compilation of early rabbinical interpretation of the Law), Galil is divided into three parts corresponding to the natural divisions of plain, hill country, and mountain. Under Roman rule, Galil was about 25 to 30 miles (40 to 50 kilometers) from east to west and about 35 to 40 miles (55 to 65 kilometers) from north to south.
Geography

The attractive Galili/Galilean landscape is made up of volcanic limestone hills and fertile alluvial plains. Its climate is cooler than that of any other part of Palestine, and its beauty and fertility contrast sharply with the barren, sun-baked hills of southern Palestine.

The physical features range from the high mountains in the north to the plain of Yizre’el in the south. Mt Tavor/Tabor is prominent on the east, while Mt Karmel stands out on the west. Much of upper Galil is 3,000 feet (914.4 meters) above sea level, and in NT times it was largely forested and less densely inhabited than lower Galil. Lower Galil starts at 1,500 to 2,000 feet (450 to 600 meters) above sea level and descends sharply to the Sea of Galil, more than 600 feet (182.9 meters) below sea level.

Besides the average annual rainfall of 25 inches (63.5 centimeters), Galil is watered by the streams that flow from springs in the hills and are the main sources of the beautiful Kishon River at Janin, and the headwaters of the Yarden River, the largest river in Palestine. The ground is also moistened by heavy dews resulting from climatic conditions created by the Levanon/Lebanon mountain range to the north.
Cities

Among the more notable cities in Galil’s early history were Kedesh in Naftali/Naphtali, a city of refuge (Jos 20:7; 21:32; 1 Chr 6:76), and Hatsor/Hazor, about 10 miles (16.1 kilometers) north of the Sea of Galil (Jos 11:10; 1 Kgs 9:15). During the time of Christ, Korazin/Chorazin (Mt 11:21) and Kafarnaoum (4:13; 11:23) were prominent cities located in the northeast near the Sea of Galil. Kafarnaoum seems to have been a center for Yeshua’s/Jesus’ ministry in the area (Mt 4:13; Mk 2:1; 9:33; etc.). Nazaret/Nazareth is especially significant as the city of Christ’s childhood (Mt 2:22-23; Lk 2:39; 4:16; etc.). Nain (Lk 7:11-17), located on the northern edge of the mountain now called Little Hermon, and Kana/Cana of Galil (Jn 2:1-11) also figured prominently in Christ’s ministry. Sepphoris and Tiberias were important cities during Roman administration.
Roads and Travel
Many roads traversed Galil, and those in NT times were superior due to Roman construction and maintenance.

Among the best-known trade routes was the Via Maris (the Way of the Sea), which ran through Galil on its way from Damesek/Damascus to Mitsrayim/Egypt. Another main road ran from Tiberias, near the Sea of Galil, to Ako/Acco (Ptolemais), a port on the Phoenician coast. Major caravan routes also connected Galil with the markets of the East. The area was tied together by a network of spurs and connecting roads that branched from the main highways.
Inhabitants

The occupants of Galil/Galilee (Galilim/Galileans) were basically Jewish in religious and patriotic orientation, but they were composed of various ethnic elements. The influence of this mixture was sufficient to cause recognizable differences in speech from that of southern Palestine (cf. Mt 26:69, 73). The Galilim absorbed more Greek and Roman influences than did the Yehudi/Jew Yehudim/Jews. The racial mixture, differences in speech, and location caused Yehudi Yehudim to view Galil and its inhabitants with contempt (Jn 1:46; 7:41, 52).

Lower Galil was densely settled with villages, and in NT times the population was probably about three million. The fertility of the soil and resultant fruitfulness of the country produced a prosperous Jewish populace, particularly in the centuries immediately after the time of Christ.
Government

Galil was under the Roman rule of emperors Augustus and Tiberios/Tiberius during the time of Christ. Roman fortifications throughout Galil were a constant reminder of the presence and influence of the Roman Empire. During Christ’s ministry, Romai/Rome installed the tetrarch Herodes/Herod Antipas (Mt 14:1; Lk 23:5-7) to rule the territory. He was appointed to office when 17 years old. Sepphoris was his first capital; in about AD 22 he built Tiberias on the shore of the Sea of Galil as his new capital, in honor of the emperor.
Products

Abundant crops enabled Galil to provide produce for the neighboring Phoenician cities of Tsor/Tyre and Tsidon/Sidon around the middle of the first century AD. Main crops included grapes, pomegranates, olives, and grains. Fishing in the Sea of Galil was a prominent business in NT times (Mk 1:14-20).
Yeshua/Jesus and Galil
Yeshua was raised in Galil (Lk 4:16), and 11 of his 12 disciples were from there (Yehudah/Judas Iskariot/Iscariot was the only Yehudi).

The culture, commerce, farming, and fishing business of the area formed the background for much of Yeshua’s ministry, as his parables show (Mt 20:1-8; 21:33; Mk 4:3; Lk 13:6-9). The first three Gospels are largely occupied with Christ’s ministry in Galil, with much of it being spent around the Sea of Galil. Most of his parables (19 of 32) were spoken here, and the vast majority of his miracles (25 of 33) were performed in Galil. Yeshua received his greatest response in this region. The Sermon on the Mount was spoken in Galil, and one of its mountains was the scene of the Lord’s transfiguration. Many of the women who followed Christ and ministered to him also came from there (Mt 27:55). Two of Christ’s most significant postresurrection appearances took place in Galil (Mt 28:16-20; Jn 21:1-23), and one of Christ’s own titles, Yeshua of Nazaret/Nazareth (Jn 1:45), identified him as a Galili/Galilean.
Galilim

Since Yeshua and most of the 12 disciples were from Galil, it was natural for the term to be applied to all of his followers, especially since it implied that the movement was not as pure as Yehudi Youdaismos/Judaism. Some interpreters believe that Luke 22:59 is an example of the use of “Galili” as a title; in Acts 1:11 and 2:7 it is merely a geographical reference. One sure reference to Christians by that title appears in the work of the pagan philosopher Epictetus (AD 50?–135?), who was impressed with how Christians died for their faith. It is not clear how common the title of Galili was, but it had obviously spread from Judea to Romai, where Epictetus lived.
See also Palestine; Sea of Galilee.

GALL
1. Yellowish-brown bitter secretion of the liver (Jb 16:13) or the organ containing the gall (20:25).

2. Very bitter, poisonous herb that cannot be identified with certainty, although the hemlock, colocynth, and poppy have been suggested. The Hebrew word occurs periodically in the OT and refers to (1) “gall” in Deuteronomy 29:18 (kjv); (2) the “poison” of a venomous snake in Job 20:14, 16; (3) “gall” or “poison” given to a person for food in Psalm 69:21; (4) divine punishment upon Yisrael/Israel as “water of gall” (Jer 8:14; 9:15; 23:15, kjv; or “poison,” rsv); (5) Yisrael’s bitter experience of divine judgment (Lam 3:5, 19); (6) divine judgment upon Yisrael sprouting up like “hemlock” in the furrows of the field (Hos 10:4, kjv; or “poisonous weeds,” rsv); and (7) Yisrael’s perversion of justice by turning “judgment into gall” (Am 6:12, kjv).

3. “Substance of an unpleasant taste” in the NT. Matthew 27:34 mentions the gall mixed with wine that was offered to Christ on the cross. Mark 15:23 speaks of “myrrh,” which may be a more specific identification of the liquid mixed with the wine. In Acts 8:23 Kefa/Peter described the spiritual state of Shim’on/Simon the magician as being “in the gall of bitterness.”

GALLIM
Village near Giveah/Gibeah of Sha’ul/Saul and Anatot/Anathoth in Benyamin/Benjamin, north of Yerushalem/Jerusalem and close to Bahurim (1 Sm 25:44; Is 10:30); probably present-day Khirbet Kakul.
GALLIO

Marcus Annaeus Seneca’s son, and brother of the philosopher Seneca, who lived from 3 BC to AD 65. Born in Cordoba, Spania/Spain, Gallion/Gallio came to Romai/Rome during Tiberios’s/Tiberius’ reign. His given name was Marcus Annaeus Novatus, but he assumed the name Gallion after his adoption by the rhetorician Lukios/Lucius Junius Gallion. The wealthy Lukios trained him for his career in administration and government.

Gallion served as Roman proconsul of Akaia/Achaia sometime between AD 51 and 53. During the apostle Paulos’s/Paul’s first visit to Korinthos/Corinth, the Yehudim/Jews brought the apostle before the proconsul, accusing him of having persuaded people to practice religion in an unlawful manner (Acts 18:12-17). Gallion abruptly dismissed the charge since it dealt with Jewish and not Roman law. His action reflected the characteristic behavior of Roman governors toward religious disputes.

Forced to leave Akaia because of illness, Gallion returned to Romai as consul suffectus under Nero. His involvement in a conspiracy against Nero resulted in temporary pardon but eventual obligatory suicide.
GALLIO INSCRIPTION*

Dated Greek inscription found in Delphi, Yavan/Greece, mentioning Gallion/Gallio as proconsul, and establishing the time of Paulos’s/Paul’s initial visit to Korinthos/Corinth (cf. Acts 18:12-17). See Chronology of the Bible (New Testament); Inscriptions.
GALLOWS

Upright frame with a crossbeam and a rope for hanging criminals. In the book of Ester/Esther, a gibbet is mentioned, upon which men were impaled and left to hang in scorn. See Criminal Law and Punishment.
GAMALIEL

1. Pedahtsur’s/Pedahzur’s son and captain or prince of Menasheh’s/Manasseh’s tribe (Nm 10:23). Gamliel/Gamaliel was chosen by Mosheh/Moses to help take the census in the wilderness near Mt Sinay/Sinai (1:10) and to organize the tribe for the journey to the Promised Land (2:20). He participated in the special 12-day ceremonial offering by the princes at the dedication of the altar following completion of the tabernacle (7:54, 59).
2. Jewish scholar. This man lived in the first century AD and died 18 years before the destruction of Yerushalem/Jerusalem in AD 70 by Titos/Titus, the Roman general.

When Kefa/Peter and the other apostles were brought before the enraged and threatening council in Yerushalem, Gamliel, who was highly respected by the council, offered cautionary advice that probably saved the apostles’ lives in that situation (Acts 5:27-40).

Gamliel is also mentioned in Acts 22:3 as the rabbi with whom the apostle Paulos/Paul studied as a youth in Yerushalem. During that period in Yisrael/Israel, a number of rabbinical schools evolved. Two of the most influential were the rival Pharisaic schools of Hilel/Hillel and Shamay/Shammai. Both of those teachers had vast influence on Jewish thinking. Hilel’s school emphasized tradition even above the law. Shamay’s school preserved the teaching of the law over the authority of tradition. Hilel’s school was the more influential, and its decisions have been held by a great number of later rabbis.

Traditionally, Gamliel is considered to be the grandson of Hilel, and he was thoroughly schooled in the philosophy and theology of his grandfather’s teaching. Gamliel was a member of the Sanhedrin, the high council of Yehudim/Jews in Yerushalem, and he served as president of the Sanhedrin during the reigns of the Roman emperors Tiberios/Tiberius, Caligula, and Klaudios/Claudius. Unlike other Jewish teachers, he had no antipathy toward Greek learning.

The learning of Gamliel was so eminent and his influence so great that he is one of only seven Jewish scholars who have been honored by the title Rabban. He was called the “Beauty of the Law.” The Talmud even says that “since Rabban Gamliel died, the glory of the Law has ceased.”
GAMMAD

Home of mercenaries who served in the army of Tsor/Tyre, according to Yehezkel’s/Ezekiel’s prophecy (Ez 27:11). Gammad may have been located in Aram/Syria and is identified as Kumidi in the Tell el-Amarna letters.

KJV form of “men of Gamadim/Gamad” (rsv) in Ezekiel 27:11. See Gammad.
GAMUL

GANGRENE*

Death of tissue due to loss of the vital blood supply to that part of the body. Often the most distal tip of an extremity, such as fingertips or toes, will turn black and surgeons will amputate the dead part to prevent extension and harm to more of the limb or to life itself.

The term “gangrene” occurs only once in Scripture (2 Tm 2:17). Paulos/Paul warns Timotheos/Timothy that godless talk will encourage more godlessness, just like gangrene tends to spread to surrounding tissues.

Although not identified by name, Asa’s disease of the feet (2 Chr 16:12) could have been gangrene. Miryam’s/Miriam’s leprosy was likened to the flesh of a macerated, gangrenous stillborn’s body (Nm 12:12).

GARDEN HOUSE*

GARDEN OF EDEN

Location in the east of Eden (Gn 2:8) in the Tigris-Euphrates area of Mesopotamia, referred to 14 times in the OT. The information in Genesis 2:8-10 indicates that it was in the Shin’ar/Shinar Plain area, and that four “heads” or branches were formed from the one river flowing through Eden to water the Garden. The heads were the Hidekel/Tigris and Perat/Euphrates (both of which are familiar modern rivers) and two rivers that have disappeared—the Pishon and Gihon. The latter were most probably natural water channels, later used as irrigation canals, since in cuneiform there is no separate word for “river” and “irrigation canal.” If Pishon and Gihon were in fact irrigation canals, then Genesis places Adamic man in an actual geographical setting and therefore obviates the notion that Eden was a myth. If the above identification is correct, Kush/Cush referred to the land of the ancient Kassites, while Havilah may have indicated Arav/Arabia.
Eden was the testing ground of man’s fidelity to God’s commands, and through disobedience, the Garden was lost. It will be regained in the form of the new paradise (Rv 22:14).

GARLIC

GARMITE

GASHMU*
