Esav’s/Esau’s grandson, the fourth son of Elifaz/Eliphaz and an Edomi/Edomite chief (Gn 36:11, 16; 1 Chr 1:36).
GATE
See Architecture; City.
GATE BETWEEN THE TWO WALLS
Entrance in the southeast part of the city of Yerushalem/Jerusalem, possibly the same as the Fountain Gate (2 Kgs 25:4; Jer 39:4). See Jerusalem.
GATEKEEPERS

Those who guarded gates of the cities and doors of palaces, temples, and other large buildings. Their task was to admit or reject visitors (2 Kgs 7:10-11; 11:4-9). In the Bible these men are variously named as gatekeepers, porters, doorkeepers, and guards.
GATH

Walled city (2 Chr 26:6) and one of the five chief cities of the Pelishtim/Philistines, which also included Azah/Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Ekron (Jos 13:3; 1 Sm 6:17), all situated on or near the southern coast of Palestine. Although frequently involved in conflict with the Israelis/Israelites, the city was apparently not subdued until David’s time (1 Chr 18:1). It was a Kena’ani/Canaanite city, the home of the giant Galyat/Goliath (1 Sm 17:4) and other men of great height (2 Sm 21:18-22). A remnant of the Anakim was left, even after the extensive campaigns of Yehoshua/Joshua (Jos 10:36-39; 11:21-22).

When the Pelishtim captured the ark of God, they carried it from Even-Ha’ezer/Ebenezer to Ashdod, from there to Gat/Gath (1 Sm 5:8), and then to Ekron. After many of the Pelishtim died or were stricken with tumors, the ark was returned to Yisrael/Israel, first to Beyt-Shemesh/Beth-shemesh and then to Kiryat-Yearim/Kiriath-jearim (6:14; 7:1). When David fled from Sha’ul/Saul, he came to Gat and feigned madness before Akish/Achish, the king of the city (21:10-15). During the rebellion of Avshalom/Absalom, 600 Gitim/Gittites served among David’s mercenaries (2 Sm 15:18). According to 2 Chronicles 11:8, Rehav’am/Rehoboam fortified the city of Gat, and 2 Kings 12:17 relates that it was taken by Hazael, king of Aram/Syria, in the ninth century. But it was apparently again in Pelishti/Philistine control when Uziyah/Uzziah broke down its walls (2 Chr 26:6). The city disappeared after being besieged and conquered by Sargon II in the eighth century BC (Am 6:2).
See also Philistia, Philistines.
GATH-HEPHER
Town in Galil/Galilee, in Zevulun’s/Zebulun’s territory, which was the birthplace of Yonah/Jonah (Jos 19:13; 2 Kgs 14:25). Modern el-Meshad occupies the site of Gat-Hahefer/Gath-hepher.
GATH-RIMMON

1. City located in the land allotted to Dan’s tribe for an inheritance (Jos 19:45). It was assigned as one of the four Levitical cities for the Kohatites/Kohathites in Dan (21:24). Lost to the Kena’anim/Canaanites, Gat-Rimon/Gath-rimmon was later regained by Efrayim/Ephraim and included as one of its cities for the sons of Levi (1 Chr 6:69). Its site is identifiable with the modern Tell el-Jerisheh.
See also Levitical Cities.

2. One of two cities given to the Levites in Menasheh/Manasseh west of the Yarden/Jordan River (Jos 21:25), suggesting a possible transcription mistake, which is better read as Bil’am/Bileam (cf. 1 Chr 6:70).
GAULANITIS*

Small province east of the Sea of Galil/Galilee, situated between Mt Hermon and the Yarmuk River and extending perhaps to the Yarden/Jordan River. It took its name from the ancient town of Golan. Archaeologists have discovered extensive ruins 17 miles (27 kilometers) east of the Sea of Galil, which they consider to be the remains of Golan. Mosheh/Moses named Golan as a city of refuge for Menasheh’s/Manasseh’s half-tribe east of the Yarden (Dt 4:41, 43), and Yehoshua/Joshua assigned it to the Gershoni/Gershonite Levites (Jos 20:8; 21:27; 1 Chr 6:71). According to Josephus, Alexandros/Alexander Janneus suffered a heavy defeat in this place and later destroyed the town (Antiquities 8.2.3). Josephus also identified a Yehudah/Judas who led a tax revolt as being from Gaulanitis (18.1.1), whereas Lukas/Luke called him a Galili/Galilean (Acts 5:37). Later, Josephus called him a Galili as well (Antiquities 20.5.2; War 2.8.1). It is quite possible that this Yehudah lived in these places at different times.

After Herodes’s/Herod’s death in 4 BC, Filippos/Philip inherited Gaulanitis, making his capital Beyt-Tsayda/Bethsaida Julias, which he had rebuilt and named after Augustus Kaisar’s/Caesar’s daughter. Yeshua/Jesus traveled in this area (Mk 6:45; 8:22), and it remained under firm Roman control until AD 66, when the Jewish war broke out. Jewish revolutionaries subsequently hid in its heights and the Romans fought several campaigns here.
See also Golan; Herod, Herodian Family.
GAZA

City near the Palestinian coast, about 50 miles (80.5 kilometers) west-southwest of Yerushalem/Jerusalem. It has been occupied almost continuously since ancient times; modern Azah/Gaza has played an important part in the conflict between Arabs and Israelis. Gazi/Gazite and Gazathite are biblical names for the residents of the town.

Set about midpoint of the length of the plain of Peleshet/Philistia, Azah was a rich agricultural area where wheat and similar grains flourished. Situated some three miles (4.8 kilometers) from the Mediterranean, Azah’s position as the greatest trading center of ancient Palestine did not come from the sea but from the highways, which brought caravans from all parts of the Fertile Crescent. This accessibility was also a handicap, for the roadways along the coast were the easiest route for the armies of Mitsrayim/Egypt, Ashur/Assyria, Bavel/Babylonia, Paras/Persia, Yavan/Greece, and Romai/Rome. Often Azah was the victim of their passage.

In the records of secular history, Azah first shows up in the annals of Thutmose III in the temple of Karnak. Thutmose wisely scheduled his Asiatic campaigns just after the Mitsri/Egyptian harvest and in time to seize the harvest of Palestine.

In Amarna Letter 289, Abdu-Heba of Yerushalem acknowledged that Azah was loyal to the king of Mitsrayim but complained that Addaya, the Mitsri ruler of Palestine whose residence was at Azah, had taken the garrison the pharaoh had sent for Yerushalem. From the late 13th century BC, there is a satirical letter that was composed as an exercise for training scribes. In this letter, written from one scribe to belittle another, various itineraries are traced, including one from the frontier of Mitsrayim to Azah.
Par’oh/Pharaoh Nekoh/Neco (610–595 BC) captured and chastised Azah and Ashkelon in the reign of Yoshiyah/Josiah and Yehudah/Judah (cf. Jer 47:1, 5).

Tiglat-Pileser/Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC) refers to Hanno of Azah, who fled to Mitsrayim just prior to the capture of Azah by the Assyrians. On the Oriental Institute Prism and the Taylor Prism, Sanheriv/Sennacherib (705–681 BC) tells of his invasion of Palestine and of how he shut up Hizkiyah/Hezekiah “like a bird in a cage.” He captured 46 of Hizkiyah’s fortified cities and gave them to three minor kings, including Sillibel of Azah, who is also mentioned by Esar-Hadon/Esarhaddon (681–669 BC) and Ashurbanipal (669–633 BC). Reference to “the king of Azah” also appears in the records of Nevukadnetsar/Nebuchadnezzar II of Bavel (604–562 BC).

In 332 BC Azah was captured and punished by Alexandros/Alexander the Great. He was angered because it had held out against him for two months, so he killed all of the men and sold the women and children into slavery. During the Maccabean period, it was taken by Alexandros Janneus, who slaughtered its inhabitants.

In the Bible, Azah is first mentioned in Genesis 10:19, where it is said that the territory of the Kena’anim/Canaanites extended from Tsidon/Sidon to Azah. In a summary of the conquests of Yehoshua/Joshua, one of the dimensions of the conquered area is “from Kadesh-Barnea/Kadesh-barnea to Azah” (Jos 10:41). Yehoshua destroyed all the Anakim in the land, but some remained in Azah and other Pelishti/Philistine cities (11:22). Another ancient people, the Avim/Avvim, “who lived in villages as far as Azah,” were annihilated and replaced by the Kaftorim/Caphtorim from Kaftor/Caphtor, or Kraitai/Crete (Dt 2:23). Azah, along with its towns and villages, was listed among the tribal inheritance of Yehudah (Jos 15:47). At the time of Yehoshua’s advanced age, Azah and the other four cities of the Pelishti Pentapolis are said to be among the territories not yet taken (13:3); in Judges 1:18-19, however, it is reported that Yehudah took it.

During the time of the judges, Midyanite/Midianite raiders swept through Yisrael/Israel, looting and destroying, even as far as Azah (Jgs 6:4). In this period the main biblical interest in Azah centers in the life and exploits of Shimshon/Samson. Pelishti women were Shimshon’s weakness. He went to Azah and found a prostitute with whom he had relations (16:1). The people of Azah learned that he was there and determined to kill him in the morning, but Shimshon arose at midnight and went to the gate of the city, took the doors, posts, and the bar of the gate and carried them to the top of a hill facing Hevron/Hebron.

His involvement with another Pelishti woman, Dililah/Delilah, resulted in his capture by the Pelishtim/Philistines, who gouged out his eyes and took him to Azah (Jgs 16:21), where he was bound and forced to grind at a mill in the prison. On a festival day in the temple of Dagon, the reveling worshipers called for Shimshon to be brought so they could make sport of him. His strength was returning, and God answered his prayer for vengeance. Shimshon dislodged the two pillars that were the support of the stone slab roof of the pagan temple, so Shimshon died, along with a great number of Gazim/Gazites.

Azah/Gaza is named as the southern boundary of Yisrael during the time of Shelomoh/Solomon, who ruled over “all the region west of the Perat/Euphrates from Tifsah/Tiphsah to Azah” (1 Kgs 4:24). Hizkiyah defeated the Pelishtim as far as Azah (2 Kgs 18:8). When he rebelled against Ashur, Sanheriv came and took 46 of Hizkiyah’s cities and gave them to the king of Azah and two other kings.

Jeremiah 47 records a prophecy against the Pelishtim, which the Lord gave to the prophet before Par’oh attacked Azah (v 1; cf. v 5; see Nekoh above). Amos gives specific prophecies of judgment against Azah (Am 1:6-7). Tsefanyah/Zephaniah also states that Azah would be deserted (Zep 2:4). Zechariah 9 gives an oracle of judgment in which it is said that Azah will suffer and that its king shall perish.

In the NT there is only one reference to Azah (Acts 8:26). Filippos/Philip, who was preaching in Shomron/Samaria, was told by an angel to go south to “the road that goes from Yerushalem/Jerusalem to Azah.” Here he met the treasurer of Kush/Cush, who was reading Isaiah 53 as he rode in his chariot. Filippos preached the gospel to this man and baptized him.
See also Philistia, Philistines.
GAZARA
Alternate name for the city of Gezer in 1 and 2 Maccabees. See Gezer.
GAZATHITES*
KJV alternate spelling for residents of Azah/Gaza (Jos 13:3). See Gaza; Gazites.
GAZELLE
Medium-sized Asianos/Asian or African antelope. See Animals.
GAZER*
KJV alternate spelling of the town Gezer in 2 Samuel 5:25 and 1 Chronicles 14:16. See Gezer.
GAZEZ
1. Kalev’s/Caleb’s son by his concubine Eyfah/Ephah, and the brother of Haran (1 Chr 2:46).
2. Son of Haran and the nephew of #1 above (1 Chr 2:46).
GAZITES*
Residents of Azah/Gaza (Jgs 16:2). See Gaza; Gazathites.
GAZZAM
Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Yerushalem/Jerusalem with Zerubavel/Zerubbabel after the exile (Ezr 2:48; Neh 7:51).
GEBA

Levitical city in the territory of Benyamin/Benjamin (Jos 18:24; 21:17), about seven miles (11.3 kilometers) northeast of Yerushalem/Jerusalem and south of Mikmas/Michmash (1 Sm 14:5; Is 10:29). It is easily confused with Giveah/Gibeah, the hometown of Sha’ul/Saul, which is also in Benyamin, to the southwest of Geva/Geba. Both names mean “hill.” The phrase “from Geva to Be’er-Sheva/Beersheba” indicated the northern and southern extremities of Yehudah’s/Judah’s tribe (2 Kgs 23:8).

In the time of Sha’ul the Pelishtim/Philistines had a garrison at Geva (1 Sm 10:5; 13:3). Yonatan/Jonathan defeated this outpost and stirred up the Pelishtim, who swarmed into Yisrael/Israel with an army vastly outnumbering the forces of Sha’ul. Sha’ul and his men were at Geva (13:16) and later approached Giveah (14:2). The Pelishtim had set up a garrison at Mikmas, just opposite Geva. Yonatan proposed to his armor bearer that they go over to this outpost and suggested that if the Pelishtim called to them to come over, that would be a sign that the Lord had given their enemy into their hand. The Pelishtim did just that, so the two Israelis/Israelites approached and killed some 20 of the Pelishtim, putting the garrison and the entire army to rout. During the reign of David, another horde of Pelishti/Philistine invaders was struck down by him “from Geva to Gezer” (2 Sm 5:25).

Men from Geva are mentioned among the Yehudim/Jews who returned from the Babylonian exile (Ezr 2:26, kjv “Gaba”; Neh 11:31). At the dedication of the rebuilt Yerushalem wall, singers from the area of Geva participated (Neh 12:29).
GEBAL

1. One of the earliest villages in Foinikai/Phoenicia and Aram/Syria (along with Ras Shamra and Tell Judeideh); also called Byblos (“books”) by the Greeks. It was situated on the Mediterranean about 20 miles (32.2 kilometers) north of modern Beirut and was an important commercial center and outlet for the hardwoods of Levanon/Lebanon in the period when it was an Mitsri/Egyptian colony and when the diplomatic and commercial interests of Mitsrayim/Egypt reached all over Aram. It was a city-kingdom according to the Amarna letters (c. 1400–1350 BC), and seal impressions found there from a very early period suggest that it was on a major exchange route through Palestine and Aram. Its inhabitants were called Givlim/Gebalites (Jos 13:5). While it was a great commercial center, a more important achievement of the Givlim was the development of a syllabic script modeled on the Mitsri. Passed on from Foinikai to Yavan/Greece, it became the ancestor of our own alphabet.
2. Territory southeast of the Dead Sea, associated with Amon/Ammon and Amalek as hostile to Yisrael/Israel (Ps 83:7).
GEBALITE
Inhabitant of Geval/Gebal (Jos 13:5). See Gebal #1.
GEBER
1. Alternate name for Ben-Gever/Ben-Geber, one of Shelomoh’s/Solomon’s commissariat officers, in 1 Kings 4:13. See Ben-geber.
2. Uri’s son, who was responsible for providing food for Shelomoh’s household. His territory was probably south of Ramot-Gilead/Ramoth-gilead (1 Kgs 4:19). Perhaps #1 and #2 were related.
GEBIM
Small town just north of Yerushalem/Jerusalem. Isaiah 10:31 prophesied that its inhabitants would flee when the Assyrian army came to invade. Its exact location is unknown.
GECKO
Small lizard, incorrectly identified with the ferret by the kjv translators in Leviticus 11:30. See Animals.
GEDALIAH

1. Ahikam’s son, and grandson of Shafan/Shaphan (King Yoshiyah’s/Josiah’s royal scribe). In 586 BC Nevukadnetsar/Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian king, appointed Gedalyah/Gedaliah as governor over the Yehudim/Jews remaining in Yisrael/Israel to work the fields, vineyards, and orchards (2 Kgs 25:12, 22).

Gedalyah established his headquarters at Mitspah/Mizpah, where he was joined by the prophet Yirmiyah/Jeremiah and the Jewish commanders and their guerrilla forces who had escaped capture during the fall of Yerushalem/Jerusalem (Jer 40:6-8). Gedalyah assured them that if they would settle down and live in peaceful subjection to Bavel/Babylon, all would be well (2 Kgs 25:23-24; Jer 40:9-10). On the basis of that assurance, many of the Yehudim who were dispersed in the Transjordan and other countries returned to Yisrael to work the land into great productivity (Jer 40:11-12).

Though warned about a plot against him by Yishmael/Ishmael, Gedalyah entertained the schemer at a meal and was killed (2 Kgs 25:25; Jer 40:11-12; 41:1-3). Along with some pilgrims visiting the temple, Yishmael fled with hostages to Amon/Ammon, escaping the vengeance of Yohanan/Johanan (Jer 41:10-15).
2. Temple musician in the time of King David (1 Chr 25:3, 9).
3. Yeshua’s/Jeshua’s son and one called to divorce his foreign wife during Ezra’s reforms (Ezr 10:18).
4. Pashhur’s son and one of the Yerushalem officials who urged King Tsidkiyah/Zedekiah to put the prophet Yirmiyah to death for his pro-Babylonian prophetic pronouncements (Jer 38:1).
5. Amaryah’s/Amariah’s son, grandson of King Hizkiyah/Hezekiah, and grandfather of the prophet Tsefanyah/Zephaniah (Zep 1:1).
GEDDALTI
See Giddalti.
GEDEON*
KJV spelling of Gid’on/Gideon, Yoash’s/Joash’s son and judge of Yisrael/Israel, in Hebrews 11:32. See Gideon.
GEDER

One of the 31 royal cities in Kena’an/Canaan, whose kings were defeated by Yehoshua/Joshua (Jos 12:13). Geder is perhaps identifiable with Gedor in the mountains of Yehudah/Judah (15:58) or with Beyt-Gader/Beth-gader (1 Chr 2:51).
GEDERAH, GEDERATHITES*

Town and its inhabitants situated in the Shefelah/Shephelah (lowland hills) of the territory allotted to Yehudah’s/Judah’s tribe for an inheritance (Jos 15:36). It was a place where potters lived (1 Chr 4:23). A man from Gederah, Yozavad/Jozabad the Gederati/Gederathite, is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 12:4.
GEDEROTH

Town (modern Qatra) in the Shefelah/Shephelah (lowland hills) assigned to Yehudah’s/Judah’s tribe for an inheritance (Jos 15:41) and later captured by the Pelishtim/Philistines from King Ahaz (2 Chr 28:18).
GEDEROTHAIM

Village in the Yehudi/Jew Shefelah/Shephelah (Jos 15:36) of unknown location. The Hebrew list contains 14 cities without Gederotayim/Gederothaim (vv 33-36), while the Greek version reads, “Gederah and her sheepfolds” (v 36). Gederotayim probably reflects a later scribal error where the copyist accidentally made the term “sheepfold” into a 15th city.
GEDOR (Person)
Yeiel’s/Jeiel’s son, who was an ancestor of King Sha’ul/Saul. Gedor’s family lived in Giveon/Gibeon (1 Chr 8:31; 9:37).
GEDOR (Place)

1. City in the Shefelah/Shephelah (hill country) allotted to Yehudah’s/Judah’s tribe (Jos 15:58) named with Halhul, Beyt-Tsur/Beth-zur, Ma’arat/Maarath, Beyt-Anot/Beth-anoth, and Eltekon. It has been identified with Khirbet Gedur north of Hevron/Hebron near Beyt-Lehem/Bethlehem.
2. Place founded by Penuel, one of the families of Yehudah (1 Chr 4:4).
3. Settlement established by Yered/Jered of Yehudah (1 Chr 4:18).
4. City and its valley settled by the Simeonites (1 Chr 4:39).
5. Town in the territory of Benyamin/Benjamin and the home of Yoelah/Joelah and Zevadyah/Zebadiah, the sons of Yeroham/Jeroham (1 Chr 12:7); perhaps the same as #1 above.
GE-HARASHIM*

Name for a richly wooded valley near Lod and Ono, settled by Yoav/Joab from Yehudah’s/Judah’s tribe, whose posterity called the valley Ge-Harashim/Ge-harashim, meaning “valley of craftsmen,” after their own trade (1 Chr 4:14, nlt mg). In the fifth century BC the area was resettled by people from Benyamin’s/Benjamin’s tribe (Neh 11:35, “valley of craftsmen“).
GEHAZI

Servant of Elisha (2 Kgs 5:25) who instructed the prophet how best to recompense the generous Shunamit/Shunammite woman for her kindness to him (4:11-17). Geyhazi/Gehazi took Elisha’s staff to use in reviving the woman’s dead son, but he was unsuccessful (v 31), and the prophet himself had to revive the child (vv 32-37). His greed in securing from Na’aman/Naaman presents declined by Elisha resulted in his contracting Na’aman’s leprosy (5:20-23, 27). In 2 Kings 8:1-6 Geyhazi again encountered the Shunamit woman as she was petitioning the king of Yisrael/Israel.
GEHENNA*

English transliteration of the Greek form of an Aramaic word, which is derived from the Hebrew phrase “the Valley of [the son(s) of] Hinom/Hinnom.” The name properly designates a deep valley delimiting the territories of the tribes of Benyamin/Benjamin and Yehudah/Judah (Jos 15:8; 18:16). It is commonly identified with Wadi el-Rababi that runs from beneath the western wall of the Old City, forming a deep ravine south of Yerushalem/Jerusalem.

The place became notorious because of the idolatrous practices that were carried out there in the days of Yehudah’s kings Ahaz and Menasheh/Manasseh, especially involving the heinous crime of infant sacrifices associated with the Molek/Molech ceremonies (2 Kgs 16:3; 21:6; 2 Chr 28:3; 33:6; Jer 19:6; 32:35). The spiritual reformation of King Yoshiyah/Josiah brought an end to these sinister proceedings (2 Kgs 23:10). The prophet Yirmiyah/Jeremiah referred to the valley in picturing God’s judgment upon his people (Jer 2:23; 7:30-32; 19:5-6).

Subsequently, the valley appears to have been used for the burning of the city’s refuse and the dead bodies of criminals. Interestingly, a well-established tradition locates the scene of Yehudah’s suicide and the consequent purchase of the Potter’s Field on the south side of this valley.

The ravine’s reputation for extreme wickedness gave rise, especially during the intertestamental period, to use of its name as a term for the place of final punishment for the wicked (1 Enoch 18:11-16; 27:1-3; 54:1ff.; 56:3-4; 90:26; 2 Esd 7:36; cf. Is 30:33; 66:24; Dn 7:10). Yeshua/Jesus himself utilizes the term to designate the final abode of the unrepentant wicked (Mt 5:22; 10:28; 18:9). Since geenna/Gehenna is a fiery abyss (Mk 9:43), it is also the lake of fire (Mt 13:42, 50; Rv 20:14-15) to which all the godless will ultimately be consigned (Mt 23:15, 33), together with Satan and his devils (Mt 25:41; Rv 19:20; 20:10).

geenna must be carefully differentiated from other terms relative to the afterlife or final state. Whereas the OT “Sheol” and NT “hades” uniformly designate the temporary abode of the dead (before the last Day of Judgment), “geenna” specifies the final place where the wicked will suffer everlasting punishment (cf. Ps 49:14-15 with Mt 10:28). The Greek form “Tartaros/Tartarus” occurs only in 2 Peter 2:4 and identifies the particular abode of the angels who fell in the primeval satanic revolt.
See also Dead, Place of the; Death; Hades; Hell; Sheol.
GELILOTH
Place mentioned in the boundary line of Benyamin/Benjamin (Jos 18:17), usually identified with Gilgal. See Gilgal #4.
GEMALLI
Father of Amiyel/Ammiel, one of the 12 spies sent by Mosheh/Moses to explore the land of Kena’an/Canaan (Nm 13:12).
GEMARA*

Summary of the important points of rabbinic discussion on the Mishnah (the oral tradition). The Gemara and Mishnah together form the Talmud (which many Yehudim/Jews consider authoritative for their faith). In Aramaic, Gemara means “acquired learning.” That meaning reflects the teaching method of the rabbis, who passed on the Gemara by committing it to memory rather than writing it down. The word’s Hebrew root means “to complete.” Since the Gemara takes the form of a running commentary on the Mishnah, it serves to supplement and complete it.

Pages of the Talmud are arranged with the Mishnah in the middle and the Gemara in blocks of print on the side. The Gemara does not necessarily quote the same sources twice when dealing with similar passages from the Mishnah on the same problem, nor does it always contain commentary on the Mishnah. The Gemara also includes folklore, astronomy, astrology, medicine, homiletic parables, and examples from great rabbis’ lives.
See also Mishnah; Talmud.
GEMARIAH
1. Hilkiyah’s/Hilkiah’s son and emissary to Nevukadnetsar/Nebuchadnezzar from King Tsidkiyah/Zedekiah. He carried Yirmiyah’s/Jeremiah’s letter to the exiles in Bavel/Babylon (Jer 29:3).
2. Son of Shafan/Shaphan the scribe. In the temple chamber of Gemaryah/Gemariah, Baruk/Baruch read Yirmiyah’s scroll (Jer 36:10-12, 25).
GEMATRIA*

One of the rabbinic hermeneutic rules for interpreting the OT. It consisted of explaining a word or group of words according to the numerical value of the letters or by substituting and rearranging certain letters according to a set system. By that rule of interpretation, for example, some rabbis have argued that Eliezer (Gn 15:2) was worth all the servants of Avraham/Abraham put together, for Avraham had 318 servants and Eliezer’s name equaled 318 (Gn 14:14). The name Bavel/Babylon is arrived at in Jeremiah 25:26 and 51:41 by substituting the last letter of the Hebrew word for the first letter of the same word.

The pseudepigraphal Epistle of Barnabas interprets the 318 servants of Avraham (Gn 14:14) as pointing to Yeshua’s/Jesus’ death on the cross, because 300 is the numerical value of the Greek letter “t,” which is cross-shaped, and 18 the value of the first two letters of the Greek word for Yeshua. In the book of Revelation the number of the beast is 666 (Rv 13:18). If the number seven is considered to be the perfect number in the Bible, and if three sevens represent complete perfection, then the number 666 falls completely short of perfection.
GENEALOGY

Record or study of descent involving a tracing backward or forward of the ancestry of a nation, tribe, family, or individual. The Hebrews were not the only people in the ancient world to take an interest in maintaining genealogical records. The Sumerian king list of the third millennium BC contains records of the early rulers of Mesopotamia. In Babylonian records the word “son” was frequently used in the sense of “descendant of.” King Tirhakah of Mitsrayim/Egypt (c. 685 BC) referred to his “father,” Sesostris III, who lived some 1,200 years before him. Greeks and Romans also kept genealogical records. However, the biblical genealogies, especially those in Genesis and 1 Chronicles 1–9, are unique in the literature of the ancient Near East. Only at the beginning of the Islamic age are such broad genealogical records found. Even today among tribal Semites, such as Aravi/Arab nomads, there is an intense interest in genealogy, and it is not unusual for an Aravi to be able to recite accurately the names of his ancestors for 10 or 15 generations back, covering a period of several hundred years.
Terms Used

The word “genealogy” occurs only once as a noun in the Hebrew OT (Neh 7:5), where it refers to a register of those who returned to Yerushalem/Jerusalem with Zerubavel/Zerubbabel at the end of the exile. The verbal form of the same word is found a total of 20 times in 1—2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemyah/Nehemiah. The terms “generations” and “book of the generations,” used in Genesis and elsewhere in the OT, convey the same idea. The equivalent NT terms are found in 1 Timothy 1:4 and Titus 3:9 (“genealogies”) and Matthew 1:1, which refers to the “book of the genealogy” of Yeshua/Jesus Christ.
Purpose of Genealogical Records

The keeping of genealogical records in ancient Yisrael/Israel was an important activity and served a number of useful purposes. God’s promise of a land to Avraham/Abraham and his descendants made such records necessary to establish and preserve the allotment of the land; a genealogical record served as evidence of a legitimate title to the ancestral property. Genealogies were essential for the preservation of the exclusive priesthood that had been established by the Mosaic law. In the time of Josephus every priest was supposed to be able to prove his descent.

One of the most important reasons for keeping genealogical records was to establish and maintain the right of royal succession in Yehudah/Judah through the family of David. The belief that the Messiah would come from the Davidic house made such records even more important.

Other purposes served by these family records included the imposition of military duty according to families (Nm 1:2-3). Position in camp and on the march from Mitsrayim was determined by tribes and families (2:2, 17; 10:11-28). Also, God’s blessings were passed from one member of the family to his descendants (Gn 27). The stress placed on the purity of the congregation (Dt 7:1-4; 23:1-8) required complete family records, particularly in the postexilic period. With the insistence of Ezra and Nehemyah upon racial purity, and with the purging of foreign elements from among the people (Ezr 2:59-63; 10:9-44; Neh 13:23-28), written evidence of purity of descent became essential; interest in the compilation of genealogies became intense after the exile.

Lineage was ordinarily traced through the male members of the family, with females being mentioned only rarely (e.g., Gn 11:29, Sarah and Milkah/Milcah; 22:23, Rivkah/Rebekah; and Nm 26:33–27:11, where the property inheritance of the daughters of Tselofehad/Zelophehad was involved). Matay/Matthew mentions three women: Tamar, Rahav/Rahab, and Ruth; and in the second group alludes to Bat-Sheva/Bathsheba (see discussion below).
Principal Genealogical Lists in the Bible

The principal sources of genealogical material in the OT are found in Genesis, Numbers, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1—2 Chronicles (which contain the greatest amount of genealogical material in the Bible), Ezra, and Nehemyah. The genealogies of Yeshua Christ in Matthew 1 and Luke 3 are the only NT records. Together they contain a genealogical record from Adam to Christ.
Grouped together by historical periods, the following are the principal genealogical lists found in the Bible:
Before the Flood

Three lists are from this period. The first, found in Genesis 4:17-22, traces the descendants of Kayin/Cain through seven generations and explains the hereditary origin of certain occupations and crafts. The second, Genesis 4:25-26, begins the account of the descendants of Shet/Seth, the posterity of Adam whose faithfulness to God is contrasted with the ungodly posterity of Kayin. The third list, Genesis 5:1-32 (cf. 1 Chr 1:1-4), traces the descendants of Adam through Shet down to Noah and his sons at the time of the Flood.
From Noah to Avraham

Genesis 10:1-32 (cf. 1 Chr 1:4-23), frequently called the “table of nations,” contains a list of the nations descended from the sons of Noah (Shem, Ham, and Yefet/Japheth). Genesis 11:10-26 (cf. 1 Chr 1:24-27) traces the descendants of Shem to the time of Avraham, and Genesis 11:27-30 (see also Gn 22:20-24) lists the descendants of Nahor, Avraham’s brother.
From Avraham/Abraham to the Descent into Mitsrayim/Egypt

The descendants of Avraham by Hagar, Sarah, and Keturah are found in Genesis 16:15, 21:1-3, and 25:1-4 (introducing the Arabs as descendants of Avraham; cf. 1 Chr 1:28-34). Genesis 19:37-38 links the Moavim/Moabites and Amonim/Ammonites to Avraham through his nephew Lot. A very important genealogical list during this period is that of the descendants of Ya’akov/Jacob, giving the account of the parentage, birth, and naming of the founders of the 12 tribes of Yisrael/Israel (Gn 29:31–30:24; 35:16-26). Esav/Esau is acknowledged as the ancestor of the Edomim/Edomites; his Edomi/Edomite descendants are traced through his three wives (Gn 26:34; 36:1-43; 1 Chr 1:35-54). The list of Ya’akov’s family at the time he entered Mitsrayim, numbering 70, is found in Genesis 46:1-27 (cf. Ex 6:14-16; Nm 26:1-51; 1 Chr 2–8). A partial list of the heads of the fathers’ houses of Re’uven/Reuben, Shim’on/Simeon, and Levi is found in Exodus 6:14-25; the chief purpose of this genealogy is to establish Aharon/Aaron and Mosheh/Moses as members of Levi’s tribe.
From the Exodus to the Conquest of Kena’an/Canaan

While the tribes were still in the desert after leaving Mitsrayim, a census was taken to determine the total number of Israelis/Israelites (Nm 1:4-54; 2:2-33). During this same period, a genealogy of the family of Aharon was compiled, and a separate census was taken of the Levites (3:1-39). A list of the 12 spies who searched out the land and the tribes they represented is given in Numbers 13:4-16; the most important names on this list are Kalev/Caleb and Yehoshua/Joshua. Near the end of the wilderness wanderings, another census of the people was ordered; the total number was approximately the same as that of the first census almost 40 years earlier (26:4-51, 57-62). As the tribes neared the Promised Land, a list was prepared of the tribal representatives who would take part in the division of the land (34:16-29).
Period of the Kings

During the entire period of the monarchy, over 400 years, the only genealogical records of any consequence are those that pertain to David. His descendants are traced through 20 rulers who sat upon the throne of Yehudah/Judah until the nation fell to the Babylonians in 586 BC (1—2 Kgs; cf. 1 Chr 11:1—2 Chr 36:21). A list of David’s children is found in 2 Samuel 3:2-5 and 5:14-16 (cf. 1 Chr 3:1-9; 14:4-7). His mighty men, an elite group of soldiers, are named in 2 Samuel 23:8-39 (cf. 1 Chr 11:10-47). His recruits at Tsiklag/Ziklag are recorded in 1 Chronicles 12:1-22. Those who were his musicians and doorkeepers when the ark was brought to Yerushalem/Jerusalem are named in 1 Chronicles 15:1-24 (cf. 1 Chr 16:5-6, 37-43). David’s political and religious organization of the kingdom—including the Levites, priests, singers, porters and other administrative officials, and military officers—is found in 1 Chronicles 23–27. In spite of the literary activity associated with the reign of Shelomoh/Solomon, the only genealogical record preserved from this period is that of Shelomoh’s princes and 12 officers (1 Kgs 4:1-19). The genealogy of one prophet is traced back four generations (Zep 1:1).
The Postexilic Period

During the postexilic period, the keeping of genealogical records probably received its greatest impetus through the activity of Ezra and Nehemyah/Nehemiah, primarily because of their insistence upon racial purity and the purging of foreign elements from the community. A list of the exiles who returned with Zerubavel/Zerubbabel is found in Ezra 2:1-70 (cf. Neh 7:6-73, where the same list is found). A list of those who returned with Ezra is included in 8:1-20. Ezra’s own genealogy is also recorded (Ezr 7:5). There is a list of the Yehudim/Jews who married foreign women that included priests, Levites, singers, porters, and other Israelis (Ezr 10:18-44). Nehemiah 8:4-7 names the Levites and others who assisted Ezra when he read the law publicly. Nehemyah also contains a list of those who participated in the ceremony of sealing the covenant (Neh 10:1-27) and a list of those who lived in Yerushalem and other cities (11:3-36). His interest in the priesthood is reflected in the list of priests and Levites who returned with Zerubavel (12:1-9), of the high priests from Yeshua/Jeshua to Yadua/Jaddua (vv 10-11), of the heads of the priestly families (vv 12-21), of the Levites and porters who served under the high priest (vv 22-26), and of the princes and priests who were present at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Yerushalem (vv 31-42).

The final genealogical record that must be mentioned is the genealogy from Adam to Sha’ul/Saul (1 Chr 1–8), the longest section of genealogical material in the Bible. It is properly included with the genealogies compiled during the postexilic period, as the unknown chronicler (some think he was Ezra) prepared this list around 400 BC from extant records and documents available to him. His purpose seems to have been to conserve the purity of blood in the restored nation and to insist that the nation’s well-being depended on its faithfulness to God’s law.
The New Testament Period
The only genealogies of consequence in the NT are those concerning Yeshua Christ in Matthew 1:1-17 and Luke 3:23-38. See Genealogy of Jesus Christ.

Matay’s/Matthew’s Genealogy (1:1-17)

Matthew 1:1 presents Yeshua Christ as “the son of David, the son of Avraham/Abraham.” By those two names, Matay highlights Yeshua’s earthly relationship to the Abrahamic (Gn 17:1-8) and Davidic (2 Sm 7:12-16) covenants of promise. Then beginning with the patriarch Avraham, Matay traces Yeshua’s human ancestry through King David to Yosef/Joseph, “the husband of Maria/Mary, of whom Yeshua was born, who is called Christ” (Mt 1:16). Matay summarizes his account: “So all the generations from Avraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Bavel/Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Bavel to the Christ fourteen generations” (v 17, rsv).
An examination of Matay’s handling of this genealogical material discloses several interesting peculiarities:
1. The arrangement of the names into three groups of 14 seems to be an artificial device.

2. To have 14 names in the second group, Matay omits three kings—Ahazyah/Ahaziah, Yoash/Joash, and Amatsyah/Amaziah—between Yoram/Joram and Uziyah/Uzziah (v 8), and one, Yehoyakim/Jehoiakim, between Yoshiyah/Josiah and Yekaneyah/Jeconiah (v 11).

3. In the first group Matay mentions three women—Tamar, Rahav/Rahab, and Ruth; and in the second group, he alludes to Bat-Sheva/Bathsheba. This is an uncommon practice in genealogies, and all the more strange when it is noted that these four represent what could be regarded as moral blemishes in the history of the Davidic dynasty— Tamar, a victim of incest; Rahav, a prostitute; Ruth, a Moavit/Moabitess; and Bat-Sheva, an adulteress.
4. In the first group Matay mentions Yehudah’s/Judah’s brothers and Zerah, Perets’s/Perez’s brother. In the second group he refers to Yekaneyah’s brothers.
5. In verse 6 David is called “the king.”

From these data, it is obvious that Matay does not intend to present a strict genealogy; the arrangement is contrived, and extraneous material is included, probably for some other purpose than merely to present Yeshua’s/Jesus’ forebears. Matay’s arrangement of the names into groups of 14, probably guided by an interest in portraying Yeshua to Yehudim/Jews as the promised king of Yisrael/Israel and rightful heir to the Davidic throne, gives a definite historical movement to the genealogy by dividing it into three periods of time. These respectively highlight the origin, rise to power, and decay of the Davidic house, the last point represented by the lowly birth of the promised heir to a carpenter of Nazaret/Nazareth.

The 14 names in each group may be an effort to call attention to the thrice-royal character of Maria’s son by focusing on the numerical value 14 of the Hebrew letters in David’s name (d=4, v=6, d=4). This number also happens to be twice the sacred number seven, so that the whole list is composed of three sets of two sevens each. It may be, however, that the contrived groupings were merely intended to aid in memorization.

With respect to the second peculiarity—the “missing name” in the third group—one must conclude that either David or Yekaneyah is to be counted twice, these being the pivotal names separating the three groups, or that a name was mistakenly dropped out in a copy of Matay’s/Matthew’s original Gospel.

The third peculiarity presents no difficulty at all. Numerous genealogies in Scripture omit some names. Ancient Near Eastern writers often used the phrase “the son of,” or the word “begat,” quite flexibly, relating grandsons or great-grandsons, for instance, to earlier forebears without indicating every intervening ancestor. The modern mind should not require a precision in ancient records that ancient writers themselves did not insist on.

The women listed in the genealogy—the fourth peculiarity—may have been intended to disarm Jewish criticism about Yeshua’s birth (1:18-25) by showing that irregular unions were not disqualifications for the Messiah’s legal ancestry.

The reason for including several brothers in the genealogy at three points—the fifth peculiarity—is not readily discernible. The mention of “Yehudah and his brothers” (1:2) may simply be following an established practice of speaking of the 12 patriarchs together.
Finally, David’s description as “the king” (1:6) underscores the Davidic or royal character of the list.

The sources employed in compiling the first group in the genealogy drew upon records preserved in 1 Chronicles 1:27–2:15 and in Ruth 4:18-22. The second group followed the records found in 1—2 Kings and 2 Chronicles. The third group relied mainly on public or private records from the intertestamental period; the nine names from Avihud/Abiud to Ya’akov/Jacob are not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture.

On the basis of this genealogy, if there had been a Davidic throne in Yosef’s/Joseph’s day, the lowly carpenter would have been the legal heir to it, and Yeshua stood after him as the next in line to inherit the royal seat.

It has been argued against this understanding of Matay’s genealogy that the presence of Yekaneyah/Jeconiah in the list (Mt 1:11) jeopardizes, if not completely negates, the legal claim to the Davidic throne of everyone descending directly from him. That is because the Lord declared of him: “Write this man down as childless, . . . for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David, and ruling again in Yehudah/Judah” (Jer 22:30, rsv). Therefore, it is said, it could not have been Matay’s intention to represent the men from Shealtiyel/Shealtiel to Yosef as legal heirs to the throne.

This is a point that admittedly could dispose of the view that the list presents David’s descendants if it were not for the fact that Shealtiyel, who in Matay’s record is represented as the son of Yekaneyah, appears also in Lukas’s/Luke’s genealogy as the son of Neri (Lk 3:27). Neri’s name is unique to Lukas’s Gospel, so it is impossible to check its use elsewhere to discover the actual parentage of Shealtiyel. But it is not surprising in the light of Jeremiah 22:30 to find him listed in both accounts with different parents. Neri most likely was Shealtiyel’s real father, and while it is impossible to determine Neri’s precise relationship to Yekaneyah, it may be that those responsible for determining and keeping the record of the legal heirs to the Davidic throne looked to the collateral line of Neri and selected Shealtiyel as the man to be legally adopted into the line and the one through whom the line would continue. Shealtiyel may well have died without a male descendant, which made it necessary to look to Zerubavel/Zerubbabel, the son of Pedayah/Pedaiah, Shealtiyel’s brother by adoption, as the legal heir to the Davidic throne. By this pair of adoptions, the curse upon Yekaneyah was fulfilled while an actual grandson of Yekaneyah continued the line, inasmuch as the grandson was legally the son of Shealtiyel, who in turn was the actual son of Neri. Yekaneyah’s presence in the genealogy is a strength, rather than a weakness, for the interpretation that Matay’s Gospel intended to present the legal heirs of the Davidic throne, since only a writer conscious of the problems surrounding Yekaneyah’s lineage, but also aware of an explanation, would present such an ancestry to a Jewish audience he was seeking to convince that Yeshua was indeed the royal Messiah.
Lukas’s Genealogy (3:23-38)
Lukas’s genealogy also has peculiarities.
1. Some expositors have thought it significant that Lukas’s genealogy appears not at the beginning of the Gospel but at the beginning of Yeshua’s/Jesus’ ministry.
2. Lukas’s account, in contrast to Matay’s/Matthew’s, begins with Yeshua and traces his lineage back through OT history. This seems irregular, for most genealogies follow the order of succession.
3. Lukas’s account, furthermore, does not end with Avraham/Abraham but goes all the way back to “Adam, the son of God” (Lk 3:38).

Some have seen the first peculiarity as a result of Lukas’s desire to bring a period of sacred history to its close, and to signal the beginning of another with the person and especially the ministry of Yeshua. The genealogy, located as it is, sets off the work of Christ from the accounts of his birth and preparation.

Many have suggested that the regressive order in the genealogy is probably Lukas’s instrument to focus attention on Yeshua. The fact that Lukas traced Yeshua’s ancestry back to Adam, “the son of God,” was probably due to the fact that he wrote for Romans and Greeks. By tracing Yeshua’s ancestry back to Adam, he shows Yeshua to be related to the whole human race. In Lukas’s genealogy Yeshua and Adam are both “sons of God”; Yeshua, of course, is the son of God by nature; Adam, the son of God by having been created in God’s image.

As to his sources, it is rather certain that Lukas used the Septuagint version (ancient Greek version of the OT) of Genesis 11:12, which inserts the name Keynan/Cainan between Shelah and Arpakshad/Arphaxad (Lk 3:36), and the records of 1 Chronicles 1–3 for the history down to David. For the period from David to Yeshua, most expositors agree that Lukas relied upon information probably received directly from Maria/Mary or from persons close to her. It was a common practice among the Jewish people for genealogical records to be maintained both publicly and privately. There was special concern in families of Davidic descent to preserve their ancestral records because of OT prophecies that Messiah would be born in the house of David.

Lukas no doubt intended to accomplish more by his list than merely a presentation of a number of Yeshua’s ancestors. Since Lukas did not highlight David in his list, it may be assumed that he was not zealous to present a list of legal heirs to the Davidic throne—not that the issue is of no concern to him (cf. Lk 1:27, 32, 69; 2:4, 11). Rather, a concern throughout Lukas’s Gospel is this emphasis—that of portraying the Christ as the Savior of Romans and Greeks—indeed, of the world. Therefore, though Lukas traced Yeshua’s ancestry through Yosef’s/Joseph’s ancestral line to David, he continued beyond David to Adam. Yeshua is a member of the race to which all people belong.
The Relationship between the Two Records

Even a cursory examination of the two genealogies of Yeshua will show several differences. For example, Matay’s genealogy comprises 41 generations, while Lukas/Luke lists 76. Lukas includes the period between Adam and Avraham; Matay does not. While the two lists are practically identical from Avraham to David, they diverge for the period from David to Yeshua, Matay tracing Yeshua’s lineage from David through Shelomoh/Solomon in 27 generations, whereas Lukas traces Yeshua’s lineage from David through Natan/Nathan, another son, in 42 generations. Furthermore, at only one point do the lines converge during this period: at the names of Shealtiyel/Shealtiel and Zerubavel/Zerubbabel, who are doubtless the same men in both lists. Finally, Matay represents Yosef as the son of Ya’akov/Jacob (Mt 1:16), whereas in Lukas’s account he is the son of Eli/Heli (Lk 3:23).
How are these differences to be explained? The differences between these lists stem from the purposes for which they were compiled and the meanings they were intended to convey.

A widely held explanation is that Matay gives Yeshua’s ancestry through Yosef and that Lukas gives his ancestry through Maria. On this interpretation Ya’akov was Yosef’s real father, and Eli (probably Maria’s father) became Yosef’s foster father, that is, Yosef was Eli’s “son,” or heir, by his marriage to Maria, assuming that Eli had no sons (cf. Nm 27:1-11; 36:1-12). This view is certainly a possibility and should not be rejected out of hand. If Maria was a direct descendant of David, it could be literally said of any son of hers, “He is the seed of David.”

On the other hand, many scholars prefer to regard Lukas’s genealogy as that of Yosef rather than Maria, since it is to Yosef’s ancestry that Lukas calls the reader’s attention (Lk 1:27; 2:4). Furthermore, nowhere in Scripture is Maria said to be of Davidic descent. If the fact that Yosef was not the actual father of Yeshua/Jesus nullifies any value that Yosef’s lineage might otherwise possess for a real son, why does Lukas point to Yosef’s lineage twice, and to Maria’s not at all?

A major difficulty for the view that regards both genealogies as Yosef’s is related to Yosef’s two fathers. One solution is that Matay/Matthew gives the legal descendants of David but Lukas gives the actual descendants of David in the line to which Yosef belonged. This would mean that Eli was Yosef’s real father and that Ya’akov was his legal foster father. How this could be is readily explainable. Assuming that Ya’akov’s father, Matan/Matthan (Mt 1:15), and Eli’s father, Matat/Matthat (Lk 3:24), are the same person, then Ya’akov (the elder) may have died without a male descendant so that his nephew, the son of his brother Eli, would have become his heir.

If Matan and Matat are not the same person, one might postulate that Ya’akov, the legal heir to the throne, died without a descendant and that Yosef, son of Eli, became the legal heir immediately upon the death of Eli and was counted as Ya’akov’s son in a list of legal heirs to the throne. Possibly Eli, a relative, married Ya’akov’s widow, thereby making Yosef, the son of that union, Eli’s son and Ya’akov’s son by levirate marriage. In other words, there are a number of possible explanations of this divergence.

One other major objection to the view that regards both genealogies as Yosef’s is that, because of the virgin birth of Yeshua, one may in no sense speak of Yeshua as being literally the seed of David—a proposition that Scripture seems to insist upon. This objection has been adequately countered: (1) because of the realistic manner in which the Yehudim/Jews looked upon adoptive fatherhood; and (2) because the relationship in which Yeshua stood to Yosef was much closer than a case of ordinary adoption, there being no earthly father to dispute Yosef’s paternal relation to Yeshua. Yeshua could and would have been regarded as Yosef’s son and heir with complete propriety, satisfying every scriptural demand that he be the “seed of David.” The question, therefore, whether Maria as well as Yosef was a descendant of David does not need to be answered one way or the other by one who desires to defend Yeshua’ Davidic descent.

It is beyond human reach to discover for certain the full solution to the divergences between the two genealogies of Yeshua, or the actual relationship of Yeshua to them. Enough has been said to demonstrate that they are reconcilable, and the purposes of each, suggested here, indicate that either of the ways outlined above does full justice to the Davidic descent of Yeshua, as rightful heir to his ancestor’s covenanted throne, and also to his virgin birth by Maria.
