Name

The name Genesis comes into English as a transliteration of the Greek word meaning “origin” or “beginning.” This name was given to the book in the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, known as the Septuagint. Genesis reflects both the content of the book and the Hebrew name for it, which is taken from its first word, bere’shith, “in the beginning.”
Author

The authorship of Genesis is closely related to the authorship of the entire Pentateuch (lit. “five-volumed,” the first five books of the Bible, which in Hebrew are called the Torah). It is clear that the Bible regards the human author of these books as Mosheh/Moses. On several occasions the Lord commanded Mosheh to write down various things: “in a book” (Ex 17:14) “write these words” (34:27). The Pentateuch reports that “Mosheh wrote all the words of Yahweh” (24:4); he wrote the itinerary of the exodus wanderings (Nm 33:2); “Mosheh wrote this law” (Dt 31:9). (Here it is not certain that all five books are meant, but it must refer to at least the greater part of Deuteronomy.) In Exodus 24:7 it is said that Mosheh read the Book of the Covenant, which he must have just completed.

The rest of the OT bears witness to the writing of the Pentateuch by Mosheh. David referred to “the law of Mosheh” (1 Kgs 2:3). In the time of Yoshiyah/Josiah, there was found in the temple the “Book of the Law of Yahweh . . . given through Mosheh” (2 Chr 34:14, nlt). Day by day Ezra read from “the Book of the Law of God” (Neh 8:18, nlt).

In the NT, Yeshua/Jesus refers to “the book of Mosheh” (Mk 12:26; Lk 20:37) and otherwise mentions the commands or statements of Mosheh (Mt 8:4; 19:8; Mk 7:10; cf. Lk 16:31; 24:44). The Yehudim/Jews also quoted from the Torah as coming from Mosheh, and Yeshua did not contradict them.

Of Genesis in particular, it may be said that Mosheh had the opportunity and ability to write the book. He could have written it during his years in Mitsrayim/Egypt or while exiled with the Keynim/Kenites. As the recognized leader of the Israelis/Israelites, he would have had access to, or perhaps even custody of, the records that Ya’akov/Jacob brought from Kena’an/Canaan. He was “instructed in all the wisdom of the Mitsrim/Egyptians” (Acts 7:22) and probably could have written in several languages and in several scripts (hieroglyphic, cuneiform, Old Hebrew). Although Mosheh was admirably fitted for the task of writing, one must remember that he was not putting together a human composition but was writing under the inspiration of God (2 Pt 1:21). We may with confidence conclude that Mosheh was the human author of Genesis.

The liberal view of the authorship of Genesis is that the book is an editorial composite—a view first put forward by a French physician, Jean Astruc, who suggested that the different names for God indicated different documents or sources for the writing of the book. The German higher critics expanded the view of the use of documents in the writing of Genesis and developed it into the Graf-Wellhausen-Kuenen, or Documentary, Hypothesis, which may also be called the JEDP theory of the authorship of the book. This view holds that there were four basic documents: (1) J, which uses the name Yahweh/YHWH (Jehovah or Yahweh) for God, dates from about the ninth century BC and comes from Yehudah/Judah; (2) E uses the name Elohim, dates from the eighth century, and comes from the northern kingdom; (3) D is Deuteronomy and is supposed to come from the time of Yoshiyah, about 621 BC; and (4) P is the priestly element, which deals with matters of the priesthood and ritual, dating to the fifth century BC or later. Some may date portions of Genesis as late as the Hellenistic period. According to this theory, the various documents were blended together by editors, so that there was a JE, JED, and so on.

The science of archaeology discredited many of the extreme postulations of these critics, and the work of W. F. Albright and his followers did much to restore confidence in the historicity of Genesis. Within the last several decades, the patriarchal narratives and the account of Yosef/Joseph have again come under strong attack, but these views are extreme, and much of the evidence adduced by Albright and earlier scholars like R. D. Wilson, W. H. Green, and others still has validity.
Date

The date of the book is also a matter of debate. Even among those who accept Mosaic authorship there is debate as to when Mosheh lived. Based on the biblical data, Mosheh should have lived in the 15th century BC (cf. Jgs 11:26; 1 Kgs 6:1), but many scholars incline toward a 13th-century date. As outlined above, the liberal view of the date of Genesis would be from the ninth to the fifth centuries BC, with the final editing coming around the fifth century or perhaps even later.
Purpose

Genesis sketches the origin of many things: the universe, the earth, plants, animals, and mankind. It gives the beginnings of human institutions, professions, and crafts. It describes the origin of sin and death, and illustrates the insidious working of Satan in human life. Above all, Genesis relates the beginning of the history of redemption with the announcement of a Redeemer who was to come (Gn 3:15). It names the early progenitors in the lineage of the Messiah and the beginning of the Hebrew people through whom the Bible and the Savior came. Genesis also gives a selective history of people and events as viewed from the perspective of the purposes of God.
Structure

The book is divided into 11 parts of uneven length, each set off by the expression “these are the generations [descendants, history] of” (2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 10:1; 11:10, 27; 25:12, 19; 36:1; 37:2). Only three times does the formula coincide with the first verse of a chapter. Usually called a heading or superscription, the expression serves as a kind of link between what precedes and what follows.
Content
The Creation (1:1–2:25)

These two chapters have been a scientific-theological battleground for many years, as researchers and students have tried to probe the origins of the universe and of life. Much of the evidence is not subject to scientific scrutiny, for science by definition requires that the evidence must be reproducible by experiment.

The statement of Genesis 1:1 remains the grandest, most precise, and most accurate statement of origins: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” He did this ex nihilo (“out of nothing”) by his word (Heb 11:3); he spoke the word of command and it was done (Gn 1:3, 6, 9, 11, 14, 20; Ps 33:6, 9).

The date of the beginning is unknown. Uniformitarian cosmogonists (students of the origins of the universe who believe that natural events have always followed a uniform pattern; cf. 2 Pt 3:3-7) have speculated that the beginning of the universe was billions of years ago. But some creationists posit a world thousands of years old.

To accommodate geological ages and the existence of extinct animals, some interpreters have proposed a gap between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2, with Genesis 1:2–2:3 representing a second or new creation. But this is conjecture. So is the idea that each day represents a geological age.

As the text stands, there is a correlation between the first three days and the second three days. Day one saw the creation of light; day four, the light bearers. Day two was the time of the creation of the firmament (better, “expanse”), which divided the waters; day five, birds and swarming water creatures. On day three, God made the dry land and plants; on day six he created the land animals and man. He made man in the image of God (Gn 1:26), “a little less than God” (Ps 8:5), and gave him dominion over the earth. He made everything “according to their kinds,” so that each kind is distinct and unique. The perfection of his work is affirmed in that “God saw that it was good” (Gn 1:4, 10, 12, 18, 21; “very good,” v 31). The seventh day was a time of cessation from the activity of creating and served as a type for mankind’s day of rest (2:1-3).

Critical scholarship eyes 2:4-25 as a doublet in conflict with Genesis 1:1–2:3. To conservative scholars, the second chapter is the same account from a different perspective. Chapter 1 gives the Creation from the standpoint of sequence; chapter 2 shows it in view of the centrality of mankind in God’s creative work.

Chapter 2 gives details of the creation of man of “dust from the ground” (v 7) and woman from a rib of the man (vv 21-22). She was created to be “a companion who will help him” (vv 18-20). They were created as mature adults, with the gift of speech and with great intelligence. Adam had imagination and vocabulary sufficient for naming all of the animal species (v 19).

The location of the Garden of Eden is given (vv 10-14). Two of the four rivers, the Hidekel/Tigris and the Perat/Euphrates, can be identified with certainty. So man lived in this beautiful garden in the bliss of innocence.
The History of Humankind from Eden to Bavel/Babel (3:1–11:26)
The Fall

The loss of Eden and the break in fellowship with God is the saddest chapter in human history. The serpent, the devil, approached Havah/Eve with the same philosophy he always uses: doubt of God’s word (Gn 3:1), denial of death (v 4), and the suggestion of equality with God (v 5). He gained access to her will by deceiving her with the promise that the fruit would make her as wise as God is (Gn 3:5; cf. 1 Jn 2:16). Havah was deceived, but when she offered the fruit to Adam, he took it willingly, knowing what he was doing (Gn 3:6; cf. 1 Tm 2:14). Later, he tried to blame God for giving him the wife who gave him the fruit (Gn 3:12). Fellowship with God was broken (v 8), yet God came seeking Adam and found him.

With sin came judgment, and the Lord pronounced righteous judgment on the serpent, the woman, and the man. The earth was also “subjected to frustration” and now groans as it awaits renewal (Rom 8:21-22). God gave hope to man and a promise of a Redeemer (Gn 3:15), who was to bruise the serpent’s head. Adam and Havah were forced out of the Garden, and it was made inaccessible to them.

The impatience of humankind is shown in Havah’s expectation that her son Kayin/Cain was the promised Deliverer. Instead, he developed a wrong-hearted attitude toward God and became so jealous of his younger brother that he murdered him. Apprehended by God and confronted with his crime, Kayin showed only self-pity and went east from Eden, where he built a city (4:1-16). Chapter 4 closes with another contrast: the brazen Lemek/Lamech, who called for vengeance, while others began to call upon the name of the Lord.
The Generations of Adam

This genealogical table (5:1-32) brings humankind to the time of Noah and the Flood. The longevity of the antediluvian patriarchs seems very striking to us, but one must remember that the earth had not yet been subjected to pollution and that the effects of sin on the human race were still nominal. The refrain “and he died” reminds us of man’s mortality. For Hanok/Enoch, however, there was something better: “He enjoyed a close relationship with God throughout his life. Then, suddenly, he disappeared because God took him” (5:24, nlt).
The Flood

With increased population came an eruption of sin (6:1-5). As men multiplied, so did their corruption. The universal condemnation of verse 5 shows a world ripe for judgment. Noah, however, “found favor with Yahweh,” for he was a righteous and blameless man who walked with God (6:8-9).

The Lord planned to annihilate the human race, but he determined to save Noah and his family. Intending to flood the earth, God instructed Noah to build an ark. Noah was directed to take animals aboard the ark, two by two, male and female, for the preservation of each species. When all was in readiness, the Flood came: “the underground waters burst forth on the earth, and the rain fell in mighty torrents from the sky” (7:11, nlt). It rained for 40 days and 40 nights. The highest mountains were covered, and life outside the ark perished. “But God remembered Noah” and sent a wind to evaporate the waters (8:1). Eventually the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat (v 4). Noah made a sacrifice to the Lord, and the Lord determined that he would never again bring such destruction upon the earth.

The Flood is another of God’s acts that has been much debated. Many have argued for a local flood, which affected only part of Mesopotamia. Archaeologists have pointed to various flood strata in the excavation of Mesopotamian city-mounds as evidence for the account of the flood and have cited the various flood stories from that area as the source of the Genesis record. The epic of Gilgamesh gives an interesting tale of this hero, who went on a mission to visit Utnapishtim, the cuneiform Noah, in quest of eternal life. The flood story told by Utnapishtim has many parallels to Genesis, but there are greater contrasts, which demonstrate that the Bible preserves the true account.

Both the Genesis account and the references to it in the NT (cf. 2 Pt 3:6) favor the view that the deluge was not a minor episode in the Tigris-Euphrates area but was an unprecedented worldwide catastrophe. Christian geologists affirm that the Flood had far-reaching effects on the earth itself. Flood stories are almost universally known, lending support to the conclusion that the Flood covered the whole earth. Following the Flood, God blessed Noah and his sons, Ham, Shem, and Yefet/Japheth. God made a covenant with Noah, promising that he would never again send a worldwide flood. As a sign of this, he established the rainbow.

Noah was the first tiller of the soil, and he planted a vineyard (9:20). Noah became drunk from wine he made and lay uncovered in his tent. Ham saw him and reported this to his brothers, who discreetly covered him. Ham and his son Kena’an/Canaan were cursed; Shem and Yefet were blessed.
The History of the Nations

“This is the history of the families of Shem, Ham, and Yefet, the three sons of Noah. Many children were born to them after the Flood” (10:1, nlt). This chapter lists the descendants of Noah’s three sons, in the order of Yefet (vv 2-5), Ham (vv 6-20), and Shem (vv 21-31). Many of the names of their descendants are preserved in tribes and nations of the world.
The Tower of Bavel/Babel

The building of the Tower of Bavel (“Gate of God”) illustrates man’s perversity and his tendency to want independence from God. The desire of man to displace God follows the fateful example of Lucifer and is a basic tenet of many cults. God thwarted the designs of the builders of Bavel by confusing their languages, so that the project came to a halt (11:1-9). The site of this tower is not known with certainty. Some associate it with Birs Nimrud, not far from the ruins of the city of Bavel. Genesis 11:10-25 picks up the line of Shem and carries it down to Terah, the father of Avram/Abram.
The History of Avraham/Abraham (11:27–25:10) and Yitshak/Isaac (21:1–28:5)

Avram came from Ur of the Chaldees, a prosperous city. The city had an imposing ziggurat (temple-tower), with many temples, storehouses, and residences. Avram and Saray/Sarai, his half sister and wife, went with his father to Haran in Aram/Syria, which like Ur was a center of the worship of the moon god, Sin (or Annar).
Avram’s Call

The call of God came to Avram directing him to leave his relatives and move to a land that the Lord would show him (12:1; cf. Acts 7:2-3). Avram obeyed. At the age of 75, he, Saray, and his nephew Lot left Haran and went to Shekem/Shechem, where the Lord appeared to him and promised that land to his descendants.

Famine drove Avram down to Mitsrayim/Egypt (Gn 12:10-20). Because of Saray’s beauty, he feared that someone might kill him to get her, so he passed her off as his sister. She was taken into the pharaoh’s harem. When the Lord plagued Par’oh/Pharaoh because of this, Avram’s lie was discovered and Saray was returned to him.
Avram and Lot

Avram and Lot returned to Kena’an/Canaan, where strife broke out between Avram’s herdsmen and those of Lot. Avram suggested that they should separate, and he gave Lot the choice of territory. Lot chose the well-watered Yarden/Jordan Valley and the cities of the plain, Sedom/Sodom and Amorah/Gomorrah (ch 13).
The Invasion of the Four Kings from the East

The four kings who invaded along the King’s Highway in Transjordan cannot be identified with certainty. Those kings were successful in their attack against the five cities of the plain, and they moved off with much booty and many captives, including Lot. Avram took 318 retainers, born in his household, and set off after them. By surprise attack, Avram recovered both Lot and the loot. On his return he was met by Malki-Tsedek/Melchizedek, king of Yerushalem/Jerusalem, to whom Avram paid tithes (ch 14).
The Covenant

The Lord promised Avram/Abram a son as heir, and in an impressive nighttime ceremony, God made a covenant with Avram and promised him the land from the River of Mitsrayim (Wadi el Arish) to the Perat/Euphrates (ch 15). Because of her own barrenness, Saray gave her Mitsri/Egyptian maid, Hagar, to Avram. Hagar gave birth to Yishmael/Ishmael, the progenitor of the Aravi/Arab peoples. When trouble arose between the women, Saray sent Hagar away, which was her right according to Near Eastern customs (as illustrated by the Nuzi tablets). God showed mercy to Hagar and promised that she would have a great posterity (ch 16).

God repeated his promise to Avram concerning his descendants and changed the names of Avram (“exalted father”) and Saray to Avraham/Abraham (“father of many”) and Sarah (“princess”). A covenant sign of circumcision was given to Avraham (ch 17). This operation had already been practiced among the Mitsrim/Egyptians for several centuries.
The Destruction of the Cities of the Plain

The Lord and two angels appeared to Avraham and announced the birth of the promised heir within a year, as well as proclaimed the impending destruction of Sedom and Amorah, concerning which Avraham bargained with God (18:22-33). Lot and his immediate family were rescued from Sedom, and the cities were destroyed by God with brimstone and fire (19:24-25). Lot’s two daughters, wishing to preserve their family line, got their father drunk and had sexual relations with him. Moav/Moab and Amon/Ammon, enemies of Yisrael/Israel in later times, were the result.
In Genesis 20:1-18, Avraham again represented Sarah as his sister and got into trouble with Avimelek/Abimelech, king of Gerar.
Yitshak/Isaac
When Yitshak was born (21:1-3), trouble again broke out between Sarah and Hagar. Hagar was driven out a second time, and once more was befriended by the Lord.
A disagreement arose between Avraham and Avimelek concerning a well, but they made a covenant of peace at Be’er-Sheva/Beersheba (21:25-34).

God tested Avraham’s faith by asking him to sacrifice Yitshak on Mt Moriyah/Moriah, which probably is the same site David later bought from Aravnah/Araunah the Yevusi/Jebusite (2 Sm 24:16-25), the place where the temple was to stand. As Avraham was about to use the knife, God called to him and showed him a ram caught in a thicket. Yitshak was freed and the animal was sacrificed in his stead.

Sarah died at Hevron/Hebron, and Avraham purchased the cave of Makpelah/Machpelah as a burial place from Efron/Ephron the Hiti/Hittite (ch 23), in a transaction typical of Near Eastern business dealings. To find a wife for Yitshak, Avraham sent his servant Eliezer back to the area of Haran, and the Lord directed Eliezer to Rivkah/Rebekah (ch 24).

Chapter 25 records the marriage of Avraham to Keturah, who bore him a number of children. Avraham died at the age of 175 years and was buried in the cave of Makpelah by his two sons, Yitshak and Yishmael.
The History of Ya’akov/Jacob and Esav/Esau (25:19–37:1)
Rivkah gave birth to twin sons, Esav and Ya’akov. When the boys were grown, Esav sold his birthright to Ya’akov for a meal of red pottage (25:27-34).

When famine came to the land, Yitshak went to Gerar, as his father had done (ch 20), and repeated his father’s lie by calling his wife his sister (26:1-11). Trouble arose with the Pelishtim/Philistines over wells, but Yitshak was a peaceable man and preferred digging new wells rather than fighting over old ones (vv 17-33).

In Yitshak’s old age, when his sight had failed, Rivkah connived with Ya’akov to trick Yitshak into giving to Ya’akov the blessing of the firstborn, which was rightfully Esav’s. This oral blessing had legal validity and was irrevocable, according to the ancient Nuzi tablets. Fearing for Ya’akov’s life at the hands of Esav, Rivkah arranged to send Ya’akov to Haran to find a wife from among her own people. At Beyt-El/Bethel, God appeared to Ya’akov in a dream of a ladder leading up to heaven; God renewed with Ya’akov the promise made to Avraham/Abraham and Yitshak (28:10-22).

Ya’akov reached Haran, found his uncle Lavan/Laban, and was employed by him (ch 29). His wages for seven years of labor were to be Lavan’s younger daughter, Rahel/Rachel, as his wife. But Lavan substituted Le’ah/Leah, so that Ya’akov had to work another seven years for Rahel. The Lord prospered Ya’akov, but he continually had difficulties with Lavan. The Lord directed Ya’akov back to Kena’an/Canaan (31:3), so he left secretly with his wives, children, and property. Lavan pursued them because his household gods were missing (possession of these “gods” made the holder heir to the owner’s estate, according to Nuzi custom). Rahel had taken them but successfully concealed them from her father, and Lavan went back to Haran.

Fearing a meeting with Esav as they passed through Edom, Ya’akov sent gifts to his brother and divided his own party into two camps for security. On this return journey, Ya’akov had an unexpected wrestling bout with the Angel of the Lord, and he was left with a limp and a new name, Yisrael/Israel (ch 32).

The meeting with Esav was friendly, and Ya’akov went on to Shekem/Shechem (ch 33), where his sons killed the male Shechemites because of the rape of their sister Dinah (ch 34). God told Ya’akov to go to Beyt-El and build an altar to the Lord. All idols of foreign gods were buried (35:1-4). At Beyt-El, God reaffirmed his promise of a posterity and the land (vv 9-15). Rahel died on the way to Beyt-Lehem/Bethlehem, while giving birth to Benyamin/Benjamin, Ya’akov’s 12th and last son. Yitshak/Isaac died at Hevron at age 180 and was buried in the cave of Makpelah by Esav and Ya’akov.
Genesis 36 records “the generations of Esav” (v 1). Here Esav is also named Edom (“Red”; cf. 25:30).
The History of Yosef/Joseph (37:2–50:26)

Yosef was Ya’akov’s favorite son and thus incurred the jealousy of his brothers. This was heightened by Yosef’s dreams of lordship over them. Their resentment of Yosef came to a climax when Ya’akov gave Yosef a beautiful coat. The brothers determined to kill Yosef, but they compromised by selling him to a caravan of merchants, who took him to Mitsrayim/Egypt and sold him as a slave to Potifar/Potiphar, an Mitsri/Egyptian captain of the guard (37:36; 39:1).

Chapter 38 relates a historic case of levirate marriage. Yehudah/Judah failed to give his widowed daughter-in-law to his third son. She deceived him into fathering twin sons and forced him to acknowledge his faults. The elder son, Perets/Perez, is named in Lukas’s/Luke’s genealogy of Yeshua/Jesus (Lk 3:33).

The Lord blessed Yosef, who soon was put in charge of Potifar’s household (Gn 39). The young man attracted the attention of Potifar’s wife, who, after many attempts to seduce him, at last accused him of attempted rape. Sentenced on this charge, Yosef met with favor in prison, where he had opportunity to interpret dreams for two of the pharaoh’s servants (ch 40). When the king had dreams that his magicians and wise men could not interpret, Yosef was summoned from jail. Yosef told Par’oh/Pharaoh that the dreams meant seven years of plenty, followed by seven years of famine. Yosef was then exalted to the office of vizier, or prime minister, second only to the king, and put in charge of the administration of the land (41:37-44).

When the famine came to Palestine, Ya’akov/Jacob sent his sons to Mitsrayim to purchase grain. Yosef recognized his brothers but did not reveal his identity to them. Yosef put them to the test by accusing them of being spies (42:9), by keeping one of the brothers (Shim’on/Simeon) hostage (v 19), and by demanding that if they came to Mitsrayim again, they must bring their youngest brother with them (42:20; 43:3). The famine became so severe in Kena’an (43:1) that Ya’akov at last allowed Benyamin to go with his brothers to Mitsrayim. The brothers were again set up by Yosef, who had his silver cup put into Benyamin’s grain sack and then had him apprehended as a thief (ch 44).

At this point Yosef revealed his identity to his brothers (45:4-15) and there was much rejoicing. Yosef pointed out that it was God who had sent him to Mitsrayim (vv 7-8), in order to preserve the lives of all the family. Ya’akov was then sent for (46:1), and Yosef met him in the land of Goshen (46:28-29). The Israelis/Israelites were assigned land in the region of Goshen, where they prospered (47:27).

In Ya’akov’s final illness, Yosef brought his two sons, Menasheh/Manasseh and Efrayim/Ephraim, to his father for his blessing. Ya’akov gave the primary blessing to the second-born, Efrayim (48:13-20). Ya’akov blessed each of his own sons and then died at the age of at least 130 years. Yosef arranged for Ya’akov’s body to be prepared for burial according to Mitsri custom (50:2-3). After the burial of their father in the cave of Makpelah/Machpelah at Hevron/Hebron, Yosef’s brothers worried about vengeance, but Yosef declared, “As far as I am concerned, God turned into good what you meant for evil. He brought me to the high position I have today so I could save the lives of many people” (v 20, nlt). Yosef died at age 110 with the prophetic request that when the Israelis went up from Mitsrayim they would take his bones with them (50:25; cf. Ex 13:19; Jos 24:32).
See also Abraham; Adam (Person); Covenant; Creation; Eve; Fall of Man; Flood, The; Isaac; Jacob #1; Joseph #1; Nations; Noah #1; Patriarchs, Period of the.
GENEVA BIBLE*
Translation of the Bible into English in 1560 in the city of Geneva, Switzerland. See Bible, Versions of the (English).
GENNAEUS*, GENNEUS
Apolonios’s/Apollonius’ father (2 Macc 12:2). Since Gennaios/Gennaeus means “noble” or “highborn,” it may be an epithet rather than a name.
GENNESARET
Area on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galil/Galilee between Kafarnaoum/Capernaum and Magdala, where many of Yeshua’s/Jesus’ healing miracles took place (Mt 14:34; Mk 6:53).

The plain of Gennaisaret/Gennesaret, as the region was called, curves along a distance of about four miles (6.5 kilometers) with an average width from sea to mountains of approximately one mile (1.6 kilometers). The topography is generally level, with the land rising slowly as it nears the bordering mountains. The unusually fertile soil is laced with flowing streams and rivers and noted for its productivity. Temperatures ranging from hot to mild allow for a long growing season and abundant crops. The fruits of Gennaisaret were so exceptional that the rabbis did not allow them in Yerushalem/Jerusalem during feast observances, fearing many would attend only to enjoy their succulence. Rabbis termed this area the Garden of God. During Yeshua’s lifetime, the area was considered the garden spot of Palestine. Trees such as the walnut, palm, olive, and fig, which require a wide diversity of growing conditions, all flourished here. Rich harvests of grapes, walnuts, rice, wheat, vegetables, and melons, as well as wild trees and flowers, were common. Later, centuries of neglect caused the plain to be largely overgrown with thornbushes, although in more recent years, certain areas have been cleared and productivity restored.
In Luke 5:1, the Sea of Galil is referred to as the Lake of Gennaisaret. The alternate name undoubtedly derived its origin from the bordering plain.
Gennaisaret (more accurately termed Gennesar) was also the later name of the town Kineret/Chinneroth (Jos 11:2), an ancient city that had long since fallen into ruin by Yeshua’s day.
GENNESARET*, Lake of
Alternate name for the Sea of Galil/Galilee in Luke 5:1. See Sea of Galilee.
GENTILES

The non-Jewish nations, known as goyim in Hebrew and ethnoi in Greek. According to the OT perspective, there are but two categories of people, the Yehudim/Jews (God’s elect) and the nations. According to the NT perspective, salvation is offered to Yehudi/Jew and Gentile alike. Both Kefa/Peter and Paulos/Paul took the lead in bringing the gospel to the Gentiles. Paulos spent his entire ministry trying to unite Jewish and Gentile Christians into one body, the church. See Nations; Paul, The Apostle.
GENTILES*, Court of the

Large outer portion of King Herodes’s/Herod’s temple complex. The court was of irregular oblong shape, somewhat broader at the north than the south. In that court, which was open to Gentiles as well as Yehudim/Jews, sacrificial animals were sold and money was exchanged. A warning was posted on a partition wall instructing Gentiles not to stray into the temple’s inner courts. Yeshua’s/Jesus’ cleansing of the temple probably occurred in the Court of the Gentiles (Mt 21:12-13; Mk 11:15-18; Jn 2:14-16).
See also Temple.
GENTLENESS

In the OT an attitude of humility or bending low (2 Sm 22:36, kjv; cf. Ps 18:35, kjv). Its adjectival and adverbial forms (“gentle,” “gently”) can mean courteous and unpretentious (Prv 15:4), quiet and tender (Dt 32:2; Is 8:6), or unharsh (2 Sm 18:5; Jb 15:11).

In the NT several words are translated “gentleness,” “gentle,” or “gently.” Shades of meaning include (1) mildness, meekness, forbearance (Mt 11:29; 1 Cor 4:21; 2 Cor 10:1; Gal 5:23; 1 Tm 6:11; 1 Pt 3:4, 15), or a courteous and unassuming attitude (2 Tm 2:25); (2) kindness expressed toward others (1 Thes 2:7; 2 Tm 2:24, kjv); and (3) fitting, fair, or seemly (1 Tm 3:3; Ti 3:2; 1 Pt 2:18). Church leaders and other believers are instructed to deal gently with those who stumble (Gal 6:1), oppose the faith (2 Tm 2:25), or are ignorant and wayward (Heb 5:2).
GENUBATH

Son of Hadad, the Edomi/Edomite prince who, as a young lad, was taken to Mitsrayim/Egypt to escape Yoav’s/Joab’s slaughter. There Hadad married a sister of Queen Tahpeneis/Tahpenes. She bore Genuvat/Genubath, who was raised by the queen as a son of Par’oh/Pharaoh (1 Kgs 11:20).
GERA
1. One of Benyamin’s/Benjamin’s sons (Gn 46:21). The name, however, does not appear in a similar list in Numbers 26:38-41.
2. Father of the judge Ehud (Jgs 3:15).
3. Shimei’s father. Shimei cursed and threw stones at David during Avshalom’s/Absalom’s rebellion; later, he sought David’s pardon (2 Sm 16:5; 19:16-18; 1 Kgs 2:8).
4. Bela’s son from Benyamin’s tribe (1 Chr 8:3, 5); alternately called Heglam in verse 7.
GERAH
Measure of weight defined as one-twentieth of a shekel, the latter being the basic weight among Semitic peoples. See Weights and Measures.
GERAR

City located in the western Negev. It was used as a geographical landmark defining the western boundary of the Kena’ani/Canaanite territory from Tsidon/Sidon to Azah/Gaza (Gn 10:19). Avraham/Abraham resided temporarily in this city, at which time he deceived Avimelek/Abimelech the king by giving him the impression that Sarah was his sister (20:1-2). Later, Yitshak/Isaac settled in this city and also disguised his marriage to Rivkah/Rebekah for fear of reprisals from the men of the city. Yitshak eventually left the town, moving to the nearby valley of Gerar on account of his conflicts with the Pelishtim/Philistines. Here the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Yitshak’s servants over a newly dug well, and Avimelek, king of the Pelishtim, made a covenant with Yitshak (26:1-26). It is doubtful that King Avimelek of Gerar (20:2) was the same person as Avimelek, king of the Pelishtim (26:8). Avimelek was probably a surname or an official title.

During the patriarchal period, Gerar appeared as a dominant Kena’ani city in the Negev; however, in Yehoshua’s/Joshua’s recounting of the Conquest, this town was not named among the Pelishti/Philistine cities yet to be conquered (Jos 13:2-3) or in the list of cities already defeated (15:21-22). Later, in the period of the kings, Gerar was mentioned as the southernmost city to which the Kushi/Ethiopian army fled before it was completely destroyed by King Asa of Yehudah/Judah (910–869 BC) and his army (2 Chr 14:13-14). Perhaps the fertile valley of Gedor (1 Chr 4:39; cf. Gn 26:17), formerly inhabited by the sons of Ham (cf. Gn 10:19), was identical with the valley of Gerar. Gedor was possibly a later scribal error where the copyist confused the Hebrew letter r for a d.

The site of Gerar is identifiable with Tell Abu Hureireh along the northwestern bank of the Wadi esh-Sheri’ah, 15 miles (24.1 kilometers) northwest of Be’er-Sheva/Beersheba and 12 miles (19.3 kilometers) southeast of Azah.
GERASA*, GERASENES

City and district in the Dekapolis/Decapolis. Gerasa was a well-known Roman city situated in the hills of the Transjordan about 35 miles (56 kilometers) southeast of the Sea of Galil/Galilee and 19 miles (31 kilometers) east of the Yarden/Jordan River. It was originally established as a Greek city by Alexandros/Alexander the Great around 333 BC. In 85 BC the Jewish monarch Alexandros Janneus conquered the city. Gerasa remained in Jewish hands until Pompey brought it under Roman control in 63 BC, at which time it was incorporated into the province of Aram/Syria and later included in the Dekapolis. The site of Gerasa is identical with the modern Jerash.

Although the city is not named in the NT, Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26-37 mention the “country of the Gerasainon/Gerasenes” (rsv) as the place where Yeshua/Jesus healed the demoniac and the swine drowned in the Sea of Galil. The parallel account in Matthew 8:28 reads the “country of the Gadarainos/Gadarenes” (rsv).

The reading of “Gerasainon” in Markos/Mark and Lukas/Luke is found in the better manuscripts of the NT over the later scribal alterations of “Gadarainos” and “Gergesenes.” Gadara was an important city of the Dekapolis whose political jurisdiction extended to the eastern shores of the Sea of Galil. It was added perhaps by later copyists to harmonize Markos’s and Lukas’s accounts with Matay’s/Matthew’s Gospel. Gergesa was a city along the eastern coastline of the Sea of Galil and the name was probably inserted in the texts of Markos and Lukas to make better geographical sense of Yeshua’s miracle. Nonetheless, “the district of the Gerasainon” has the best textual support and should be understood as the intended site of Markos and Lukas for Yeshua’s exorcism and miracle. To the non-Palestinian Roman and Greek readers of Markos and Lukas’s Gospels, the small regional district of Gadara would be unknown; however, the affluent Roman city of Gerasa would be widely known and suitable as a geographical designation for Yeshua’s miracle at the Sea of Galil.
See also Decapolis; Gadara, Gadarenes; Girgashites.
GERGESA*, GERGESENES*

City on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galil/Galilee. Gergesa is near Gadara, probable site of Yeshua’s/Jesus’ miracle of healing a demon-possessed man and casting the demons into a nearby herd of swine. Though the account of this miracle in Matthew 8:28 refers to the “country of the Gergesenes” (kjv), it is most likely that Matay/Matthew used the reference to Gergesa as a regional identifier rather than a specific location. See Gadara, Gadarenes; Gerasa, Gerasenes.
GERIZIM, Mount

Mountain (modern Jebel et-Tor) from which the blessings were to be pronounced, just as the cursings were to come from Mt Eyval/Ebal (Dt 11:29). The two mountains designated by God were opposite each other, and the setting was a memorable one with six tribes positioned on Mt Gerizim and six on Mt Eyval, the Levites standing in the valley between—reciting the blessings and the cursings (Dt 27:11–28:68; Jos 8:33-35). The mountain is near Shekem/Shechem, about 10 miles (16.1 kilometers) southeast of the city of Shomron/Samaria, and it is referred to by the woman of Shomron in John 4:20-23 as the mountain where “our fathers worshiped.” Avraham/Abraham, indeed, had built an altar in this area (Gn 12:6-7; 33:18-20), and it had been the revered site for Shomroni/Samaritan worship for centuries. Yeshua/Jesus responds to the woman by pointing out that the physical locality of worship (whether Gerizim or Yerushalem/Jerusalem) is not important—the spirtual reality is. One must worship in spirit and in truth.

It was in this area that the bones of Yosef/Joseph were buried (Jos 24:32) and that Yehoshua/Joshua called upon the people to renew their allegiance to the God of their fathers (vv 25-27). Josephus records in his Antiquities (11.8.2-4) Sanvalat’s/Sanballat’s promise to Menasheh/Manasseh to preserve for him the honor of the priesthood and also to build a temple on Mt Gerizim like that at Yerushalem. It was apparently destroyed later by the Maccabean forces under Hurkanos/Hyrcanus (Antiquities 13.9.1). The Shomronim/Samaritans still worship at Nablus, which lies at the foot of Mt Gerizim, but are a diminishing community precariously held together.
GERON*
Athainaios/Athenian senator who compelled the Yehudim/Jews to forsake the laws of their fathers and their God during the time of Antiokos/Antiochus IV Epifanes/Epiphanes (2 Macc 6:1, rsv mg).
GERSHOM
1. Mosheh’s/Moses’ son by Tsiporah/Zipporah, born in Midyan/Midian during Mosheh’s exile from Mitsrayim/Egypt (Ex 2:22; 18:3; 1 Chr 23:15-16).
2. Yonatan’s/Jonathan’s father. He and his sons were priests to Dan’s tribe. The Danim/Danites set up a graven image to worship and appointed Yonatan to be their priest (Jgs 18:30).
3. Alternate spelling of Gereshon/Gershon, Levi’s oldest son (1 Chr 6:1, 16-17, 20, 43; 23:6-7). See Gershon, Gershonites.
4. Ancestor of Shevuel/Shebuel, the chief officer over the temple treasury during David’s reign (1 Chr 26:24).
5. Pinhas’s/Phinehas’ son who returned with Ezra after the exile (Ezr 8:2).
GERSHON, GERSHONITES

Levi’s oldest son (also spelled Gereshom/Gershom) who went into Mitsrayim/Egypt with Yisrael/Israel (Gn 46:11; Nm 3:17; 1 Chr 6:1) and was ancestor of a division of Levites (Gershonim/Gershonites) who came out of Mitsrayim with Mosheh/Moses (Ex 6:16-17; Nm 3:18, 21).

In the list of the allotment of Levitical cities, the Gershonim were listed as one of the largest Levitical groups in Yisrael (Jos 21:1-7). Some passages indicate that they were at times dominant among the functioning Levitical groups (Gn 46:11; Ex 6:16; Nm 3:17; 26:57; 1 Chr 6:1, 16; 23:6).

According to the book of Numbers, the Gershonim were encamped behind the tabernacle to the west during the wilderness wanderings (Nm 3:23). Early in the second year after the exodus from Mitsrayim, the Gershoni/Gershonite males numbered about 7,500 (v 22). Only those between the ages of 30 and 50 could serve in the tabernacle, which at the time of that early census totaled 2,630 men (4:39-40). They were responsible for the care and transportation of the external furnishings of the tabernacle (3:25-26; 4:24, 27-28) and were given two wagons and four oxen for the purpose, being supervised by Aharon/Aaron and his sons (4:27).

After the initial settlement of Kena’an/Canaan, the Gershonim were allotted 13 cities among the tribes of Yisakar/Issachar, Asher, Naftali/Naphtali, and Menasheh/Manasseh in the northern part of Palestine (Jos 21:6).

During the time of King David, they were listed among the Levites appointed to service in the temple (1 Chr 23:6-11). The Gershoni families of Laedan/Ladan and Yehiel/Jehieli were in charge of the treasury of the house of God (26:20-22). At David’s request, music in the temple was directed in part by Asaf/Asaph and his family, who were Gershonim (25:1-2). In the reign of King Hizkiyah/Hezekiah the Gershonim are mentioned among the Levites who cleansed the temple (2 Chr 29:1-6, 12). In the postexilic period the descendants of Asaf celebrated the laying of the temple foundation (Ezr 3:10) and the dedication of the city walls (Neh 12:31-36) with music.
See also Levi, Tribe of; Priests and Levites.
GERUTH-KIMHAM

Plot of land (meaning “the lodging place of Kimham”) near Beyt-Lehem/Bethlehem. Geruth-kimham possibly was given to Kimham for the service that his father, Barzilay/Barzillai the Giladi/Gileadite, had rendered to King David (2 Sm 19:31-40; 1 Kgs 2:7). After the fall of Yerushalem/Jerusalem (586 BC), Geruth-kimham was the camp of Yohanan/Johanan son of Kareah and his men as they prepared to flee to Mitsrayim/Egypt (Jer 41:17). See Kimham.
GESHAN
Yehday’s/Jahdai’s son and a descendant of Yehudah/Judah through Kalev’s/Caleb’s line (1 Chr 2:47).
GESHEM

Aravi/Arab opponent of Nehemyah/Nehemiah who derided those seeking to rebuild the walls of Yerushalem/Jerusalem (Neh 2:19; 6:1-6). He was likely an inhabitant of the north Aravi Desert and has been identified with Gashmu son of Shahr in a Dedani/Dedanite Aravi inscription. Like Sanvalat/Sanballat and Toviyah/Tobiah, his economic interests were threatened by the rebuilding of Yerushalem.
GESHUR, GESHURITES

1. District and its inhabitants east of the Yarden/Jordan River, in the tribal allotment of the half-tribe of Menasheh/Manasseh (Jos 13:11). Most Bible geographers place it near Bashan, on the northeast shore of the Sea of Galil/Galilee. In their conquest of the land, the Israelis/Israelites defeated Og, king of Bashan, and Yair/Jair of Menasheh took Bashan as far as the border of the Geshurim/Geshurites and Ma’akatim/Maacathites (Dt 3:14). Though the land of the Geshurim was given to the Transjordanian tribes (Jos 13:11), Yisrael/Israel did not drive them out (v 13). Later, Geshur and Aram took at least 60 towns from the Israelis in Transjordan (1 Chr 2:23).

David married Ma’akah/Maacah, daughter of Talmay/Talmai, king of Geshur, and she bore Avshalom/Absalom (2 Sm 3:3; 1 Chr 3:2). After the vengeful murder of Amnon, Avshalom fled to Geshur for refuge with his grandfather, Talmay (2 Sm 13:37) and stayed there three years.
See also Syria, Syrians.

2. Name of an area and its people south of Peleshet/Philistia. Among the lands not yet taken at the time of Yehoshua’s/Joshua’s advanced old age are listed “all the regions of the Pelishtim/Philistines and Geshurim: from the Shihor River on the east of Mitsrayim/Egypt to the territory of Ekron on the north” (Jos 13:2-3, niv). When David lived at Tsiklag/Ziklag, in the territory of Akish/Achish, king of Gat/Gath, David made raids upon the Geshurim and others “as far as Shur, to the land of Mitsrayim” (1 Sm 27:8).
GETHER
Aram’s son and the grandson of Shem (Gn 10:23). In 1 Chronicles 1:17 he is listed as one of the sons of Shem.
GETHSEMANE

Place to which Yeshua/Jesus and his disciples walked after their Last Supper together in the upper room. In Gethsaimanai/Gethsemane, Yeshua underwent a great inner struggle, as he realized the hour of his betrayal was at hand (Mt 26:36-56; Mk 14:32-50; Lk 22:39-53).

The name Gethsaimanai, used only in the Gospels of Matay/Matthew (26:36) and Markos/Mark (14:32), means “oil press,” suggesting the presence of an olive grove. The use of the Greek word “place” in the Gospel accounts indicates that Gethsaimanai was an enclosed piece of ground. It may be that the grove was privately owned and that Yeshua and his disciples had special permission to enter.

Though the Gospels of Lukas/Luke and Yohan/John do not mention the word Gethsaimanai, they both record Yeshua’s agony before his betrayal. Lukas says the location was on the “Mount of Olives” (Lk 22:39). Yohan describes the area as “across the Kidron Valley” (Jn 18:1); Yohan’s is the only Gospel to call the spot a garden. From those accounts it is also evident that Yeshua and his disciples gathered in Gethsaimanai often for fellowship and prayer (Lk 22:39; Jn 18:2). The Gospel narratives indicate that the garden was large enough for the group to separate into different parts of it.
GEUEL
Maki’s son from Gad’s tribe, and one of the 12 spies appointed by Mosheh/Moses to search out the Promised Land of Kena’an/Canaan (Nm 13:15).
GEZER

Modern Tell Yetser/Jezer (also known as Tell Abu Shusha), and an important ancient city in a strategic position in the north Shefelah/Shephelah hills. The city of the third millennium BC was protected by a brick wall, which was replaced by a 13-foot- (4-meter-) thick stone wall. The Kena’ani/Canaanite city reached its zenith during the 20th to 14th centuries BC. The so-called outer wall was 14 feet (4.3 meters) thick and enclosed an area of 27 acres. There was a Kena’ani high place (c. 1600 BC) with 10 pillars or standing stones (up to 10 feet, or 3 meters, high) and a stone altar or basin. A 216-foot (65.8-meter) tunnel with steps led down to a spring in a cave, so that there was safe and ready access to water in time of siege, as at Giveon/Gibeon and other Palestinian sites. Objects found indicate cultural and commercial contacts with Mitsrayim/Egypt. The Gezer Calendar, a stone tablet with a Hebrew inscription that gives the months of the year in terms of agricultural activities, has been dated to the 10th century BC.

Horam, the king of Gezer, was defeated by the Israelis/Israelites under Yehoshua/Joshua (Jos 10:33). Gezer was a Levitical city in the tribal territory of Efrayim/Ephraim (16:3; 21:21), but Efrayim was unable to drive out the Kena’anim/Canaanites (Jgs 1:29). Merneptah (c. 1225–1215 BC) of Mitsri/Egyptian dynasty 19 lists Gezer, along with Ashkelon and Yanoam, on the Yisrael/Israel Stele, which gives an account of his conquests.

During the reign of David, the Pelishtim/Philistines invaded the plain of Refaim/Rephaim, but the Lord instructed David in a successful ambush and David struck down the Pelishtim “from Geva/Geba to Gezer” (2 Sm 5:25).

After Shelomoh’s/Solomon’s marriage to the daughter of the king of Mitsrayim, the pharaoh, whose identity is uncertain, captured and burned Gezer and gave it as a dowry to his daughter (1 Kgs 9:16). Shelomoh rebuilt Gezer, along with a number of other cities that served as store-cities or chariot-cities (cf. vv 15-19). He fortified Gezer and made a strong gate with four sets of piers, like those at Hatsor/Hazor and Megidon/Megiddo.

In the fifth year of Rehav’am’s/Rehoboam’s reign, Shishak (Sheshonk), king of Mitsrayim, invaded Yisrael (1 Kgs 14:25). Gezer is included in the list of captured cities inscribed on the wall of the temple of Karnak.

The capture of Gezer by the Assyrian king Tiglat-Pileser/Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC) was shown in reliefs on the walls of his palace at Nimrud (biblical Kelah/Calah). The Assyrians brought to Gezer conquered people from other areas, as they did at Shomron/Samaria (2 Kgs 17:24). Cuneiform tablets of contracts testify to their presence.
See also Levitical Cities.
GEZRITE*
KJV spelling of Gizri/Girzite in 1 Samuel 27:8. The Gizrim/Girzites were raided by David’s men while he was at Tsiklag/Ziklag. See Girzites.
GHOST*, Holy
See Holy Spirit.
GIAH
Unidentified place along the descent from Giveon/Gibeon to the Aravah/Arabah to which Yoav/Joab and Avishay/Abishai pursued Avner/Abner (2 Sm 2:24).
GIANTS

English translation of four different Hebrew words. One of these words occurs in Job 16:14, where the Hebrew word is translated “warrior” in the rsv, and “giant” in the kjv. Another Hebrew word is translated “giants” in the nlt and “Nefilim/Nephilim” (a transliteration of the Hebrew) in the rsv (Gn 6:4; Nm 13:33). The original meaning of this Hebrew term is unknown, but it seems to be used of a group or race of people. Since none of the terms translated “giants” has that actual meaning, we cannot be sure that the Nefilim were of unusual physical stature.

In several passages the kjv translates “giants” and the rsv translates “Refaim/Rephaim” (e.g., Dt 2:20; 3:11; Jos 12:4). That word, usually in plural form, refers to several tribes of people who inhabited Palestine and who may have been unusually large in physical size. They included the Anakim of Yehudah’s/Judah’s coastal area and hill country around Hevron/Hebron (Dt 2:11), the Emim of Moav/Moab (v 10), the Zamzummim of Amon/Ammon (v 20), and the inhabitants of Bashan (3:11). The word also appears in Yehoshua/Joshua (Jos 12:4; 13:12; 15:8; 17:15; 18:16). Some interpreters have suggested that these people were the original inhabitants of Palestine who were distinct tribes of tall people and who were eventually conquered and absorbed by the Kena’anim/Canaanites, Pelishtim/Philistines, Hebrews, and other invading peoples. Other interpreters contend that they were not distinct racial tribes but were individuals of great stature, perhaps the result of disease, who were found among the various races and tribes of Palestine. Neither contention can be established with certainty. Another Hebrew term is translated “giant” in both the kjv and nlt (2 Sm 21:16-22; 1 Chr 20:4-8).

Perhaps the most famous giant in biblical literature is Galyat/Goliath of Gat/Gath, the Pelishti/Philistine soldier who challenged King Sha’ul’s/Saul’s army at the valley of Elah and caused them to be dismayed and afraid (1 Sm 17). He is said to have been six cubits and a span tall, which has been variously interpreted as being between seven and a half and nine and a half feet (2.3 to 2.9 meters). David’s defeat of Galyat brought the youth prominence in Yisrael/Israel (18:5-7). Galyat is not referred to in the text as a “giant,” but his height marks him as one of gigantic size. King Og of Bashan was another unusually tall person (Dt 3:11).
See also Nephilim.
GIANTS*, Valley of the
KJV translation for “valley of Rephaim” in Joshua 15:8 and 18:16. See Rephaim, Valley of.
GIBBAR

Forefather of a family that returned to Yerushalem/Jerusalem with Zerubavel/Zerubbabel (Ezr 2:20). The parallel list in Nehemiah 7:25 reads “sons of Giveon/Gibeon,” suggesting that “Givar/Gibbar” may be a textual corruption. Some support for this view lies in the fact that Ezra 2:21 begins listing descendants by their home city rather than by family.
GIBBETHON

City in the western part of central Palestine. It was located in the territory of Dan (Jos 19:44) and allotted to the Levite clan of Kohat/Kohath (21:23). Baesha/Baasha killed King Nadav/Nadab at Gibton/Gibbethon when Yisrael/Israel was taking the city from the Pelishtim/Philistines (1 Kgs 15:27). About 26 years later, Omri was proclaimed king at Gibton (16:17).
See also Levitical Cities.
GIBEA
Kalev’s/Caleb’s grandson from Yehudah’s/Judah’s tribe (1 Chr 2:49).
GIBEAH

1. Town in the hill country of Yehudah/Judah (Jos 15:57). Its exact location is uncertain. Giveah/Gibeah is listed as being among other towns located in the section of Yehudah southeast of Hevron/Hebron and probably was in the fertile plateau containing Maeon/Maon, Zif/Ziph, and Karmel/Carmel.

2. Town in the province of Benyamin/Benjamin, also called “Giveah of Sha’ul/Saul” (1 Sm 11:4; 15:34; Is 10:29), and its inhabitants are called Gibeathites (1 Chr 12:3). It is first mentioned in the description of the territory assigned to Benyamin (Jos 18:28, kjv “Gibeath”) and comes to prominence in the biblical narrative as a result of the atrocity recounted in Judges 19–21 of the Levite and his concubine.

Giveah was also noted as the home of Sha’ul (1 Sm 10:26). After his anointing as king of Yisrael/Israel, Sha’ul returned to Giveah, which probably remained his home and his capital (10:26; 22:6; 23:19).

The site of ancient Giveah has been generally identified as the modern Tell el-Ful. The OT references place Giveah north of Yerushalem/Jerusalem, between Yerushalem and Ramah, and situated near the primary south-north road through the hill country (Jgs 19:11-19). Tell el-Ful is about three and a half miles (5.6 kilometers) north of Yerushalem and is situated on one of the highest areas in that mountain range. Excavations reveal that an early Israeli/Israelite village was there about the 12th century BC and was destroyed by fire. Probably during the 11th century a stone fortress was built, and its corner tower is still evident. It probably was the citadel of Sha’ul and his royal residence. A second fortress was built about 1000 BC but fell into disuse when David established the Israeli capital at Yerushalem. It then served as an outpost for the capital city. The tower was alternately destroyed and rebuilt through the centuries until its final destruction in the war between Antiokos/Antiochus III and Ptolemaios/Ptolemy V. Josephus wrote that a village existed at the site of Giveah during the Roman period, but it finally ceased to exist with the Roman destruction of Yerushalem (AD 70).

3. Town in the hills of Efrayim/Ephraim that was given to Pinhas/Phinehas, son of Eleazar. It was the burial site of Eleazar (Jos 24:33). An addition to the Septuagint indicates that Pinhas was also buried here. Its exact location is unknown, and several sites have been suggested: Nibi Saleh, about six miles (9.7 kilometers) northwest of Jifna; Jibia, four miles (6.5 kilometers) northwest of Jifna; et-Tell, northeast of Jifna and south of Sinjil; and Awertah, near Shekem/Shechem.

4. Givat-Elohim/Gibeath-elohim (1 Sm 10:5, rsv; kjv “hill of God”; nlt “Giveah of God”). At this site Shmuel/Samuel, following Sha’ul’s anointing as king, predicted that Sha’ul would meet a company of prophets and would prophesy with them. This was to be a sign of God’s selection of Sha’ul as Yisrael’s king. Some have suggested that this is the same place as Giveah of Benyamin, the home of Sha’ul, but the context suggests that Sha’ul reached this place before he arrived at his home.

5. Hill near Kiryat-Yearim/Kiriath-jearim, where the ark of the covenant was housed by Avinadav/Abinadab after its return from the Pelishtim/Philistines and until it was moved by David to the house of Oved-Edom/Obed-edom (2 Sm 6:1-4).
GIBEATH*
KJV spelling of the town Giveah/Gibeah in Joshua 18:28. See Gibeah #2.
GIBEATH-ELOHIM*
Place where Shmuel/Samuel foretold an event that would confirm Sha’ul/Saul as Yisrael’s/Israel’s king (1 Sm 10:5, rsv; nlt mg). See Gibeah #4.
GIBEATH-HAARALOTH

Place located between the Yarden/Jordan River and Yeriho/Jericho, in the vicinity of Gilgal, where Yehoshua/Joshua conducted the circumcision of the Hebrew males born in the wilderness during the 40 years of wandering. (Jos 5:3, nlt; kjv “hill of the foreskins”).
GIBEATHITE*
Inhabitant of the Benyamite/Benjamite town of Giveah/Gibeah (1 Chr 12:3). See Gibeah #2.
GIBEON, GIBEONITES

Place and its inhabitants figuring prominently in the OT from the days of Yehoshua/Joshua to the days of Nehemyah/Nehemiah, though both were in existence outside these time limits. The site may be identified with confidence as el-Jib some five and a half miles (8.9 kilometers) north of Yerushalem/Jerusalem. This identification was proposed as early as 1838 by Edward Robinson. Since the excavation of this site in the years 1956, 1957, 1959, 1960, and 1962, and the discovery of 31 jar handles bearing the name of Giveon/Gibeon, the identification is placed beyond doubt. Certain geographical and chronological considerations also support this. The location of Giveon, north of Yerushalem and accessible to that city in the days of David, Shelomoh/Solomon, and Yirmiyah/Jeremiah, as well as its location southwest of Ay/Ai combine geographically to support this identification. Further, the periods of occupation at el-Jib revealed by excavation are parallel to historical data supplied by the OT.

The first mention of Giveon and its inhabitants comes in Joshua 9 and 10 in the days of Yehoshua, perhaps about 1200 BC. Hearing of the success of the people of Yisrael/Israel at Yeriho/Jericho and Ay, the people of Giveon, Kefirah/Kephirah, Be’erot/Beeroth, and Kiryat-Yearim/Kiriath-jearim plotted to obtain a covenant of peace from them. By pretending that they had come from afar and displaying worn-out clothing and footwear as well as dried bread, they were able to deceive Yehoshua into making a treaty with them. When their deception was discovered, they were sentenced to chop wood and carry water for the Israelis/Israelites (Jos 9:21-27). Neighboring groups of people from Yerushalem, Hevron/Hebron, Yarmut/Jarmuth, Lakish/Lachish, and Eglon, led by Adoni-Tsedek/Adoni-zedek king of Yerushalem, launched an attack on Giveon because of its defection to Yehoshua. The Givonim/Gibeonites appealed to Yehoshua, and the Israelis made a forced march from Gilgal to assist them. The enemies of Giveon were driven down the road to Beyt-Horon/Beth-horon. Their rout was completed with the assistance of hailstones. In that day the sun stood still over Giveon (10:9-13). Only Giveon made peace with the incoming Israelis (11:19). In due course the town became part of Benyamin’s/Benjamin’s territory (18:25; 21:17).

In the days before David was king, Sha’ul’s/Saul’s general encountered some of David’s men at Giveon and engaged in an unusual contest at the pool of Giveon. Twelve men from each side fought and were all thrust through by the swords of their opponents (2 Sm 2:12-17). This encounter was followed by a further skirmish in which David’s men were successful (vv 18-32). Later, David’s nephew Amasa, captain of the rebel army of Avshalom/Absalom, was attacked by Yoav/Joab at the “great stone which is in Giveon” (20:8) and left to die in the highway in his blood. In David’s time also, seven sons of Sha’ul were executed “at Giveon on the mountain of the Lord” (21:1-9) in retribution for Sha’ul’s violation of the ancient covenant between Giveon and Yisrael when he slew men of Giveon (vv 1-6).

There was an important high place still operating at Giveon in David’s time. The tabernacle of the Lord rested there, and an altar of burnt offering as well (1 Chr 16:39; 21:29). It was at Giveon, according to 1 Kings 3:3-9, that Shelomoh had a dream in which Shelomoh asked for wisdom to govern Yisrael well (cf. 2 Chr 1:2-13). A second time God appeared to Shelomoh at Giveon to assure him that his prayer had been heard and to urge him to walk in God’s ways (1 Kgs 9:2-9). Giveon was among the cities taken by Par’oh/Pharaoh Shishak in the second half of the 10th century BC. Presumably Giveon remained an important center during the days of the kings. There was a prophet in Giveon in the days of Yirmiyah, although he prophesied falsely (Jer 28:1-4).

Some of the Givonim went into exile in Bavel/Babylon and a small group returned (Neh 7:25) and assisted Nehemyah in repairing the Yerushalem wall (3:7-8). Later still, Josephus relates that Cestius pitched his camp at Giveon on his march to Yerushalem in AD 66 (War 2.515-516). Biblical references cover a period from about 1200 BC to about 445 BC, in archaeological terms from the beginning of the Iron I period, through the Iron II period, and into the Persian or Iron III period. We would expect, therefore, to find evidence for at least these periods in an excavation.
See also Conquest and Allotment of the Land; Gibbar.
GIBLITE*
KJV rendering of Givli/Gebalite, an inhabitant of Geval/Gebal, in Joshua 13:5. See Gebal #1.
GIDDALTI*

Heyman’s/Heman’s son and a temple singer appointed by David to serve under the direction of his father (1 Chr 25:4). The 22d of the 24 divisions of service was appointed to Gidalti/Giddalti (1 Chr 25:29, nlt mg).
GIDDEL
1. Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Yerushalem/Jerusalem with Zerubavel/Zerubbabel after the exile (Ezr 2:47; Neh 7:49).
2. Ancestor of a group of King Shelomoh’s/Solomon’s servants who returned with Zerubavel after the Babylonian exile (Ezr 2:56; Neh 7:58).
GIDEON

Judge of Yisrael/Israel, son of Yoash/Joash, of the clan of Aviezer/Abiezer and the tribe of Menasheh/Manasseh. Of the 12 judges of Yisrael, more verses are devoted to Gid’on/Gideon than any other—Shimshon/Samson running a close second. The narrative in which he is the central character antedates the Christian era by roughly 11 centuries.

Following seven years of cruel oppression by the Midyanites/Midianites, Yisrael cried out to the Lord for relief (Jgs 6:6). An unknown prophet informs the Israelis/Israelites that their miserable conditions stem from their forgetting to give exclusive devotion to the one true God. God sends his angel to Gid’on. A touch of humor earmarks the angel’s greeting, for the “mighty warrior” (v 12) is threshing wheat secretly for fear of the Midyanites. Yet God addresses Gid’on in realization of what his mighty power is able to accomplish in him (vv 14-16, 34). Conscious of his own weakness and the formidable task before him, Gid’on is an ideal vehicle for God’s tremendous work of deliverance (cf. 1 Cor 1:27; 2 Cor 12:10).

Gid’on’s first task is to tear down his father’s altar to Ba’al/Baal and the adjacent one to Asherah, Ba’al’s female consort (cf. Is 42:8). Knowing that the people would resist such an act, Gid’on and his servants destroy these images of debased Kena’ani/Canaanite religion at night. The following day the men of Ofrah/Ophrah confront Gid’on and seek his life in retaliation for the act. Yoash pleads the cause of his son, inviting Ba’al, if he indeed is deity, to contend for himself. Out of this confrontation the name Yeruba’al/Jerubbaal (“let Ba’al contend”) is ascribed to Gid’on (Jgs 6:32).

Yet Gid’on is a man of inconstant faith, and his desire of further assurance is not rebuked as God graciously and patiently accedes to his requests concerning the dew and the fleece (Jgs 6:36-40). Subsequently Gid’on is informed that mere numbers will not assure victory. Moreover, there must be no doubt whatever as to the true source of Yisrael’s liberation (7:2). From 32,000, Gid’on’s troops are trimmed down to only 300 by an unusual method of reduction (vv 3-7). A secret reconnaissance mission to the outskirts of the oppositions’ camp enables Gid’on to receive further strengthening as he and his servant Purah overhear a Midyanite/Midianite soldier reveal his dream indicating Yisrael’s imminent victory (vv 13-14). In response to this additional encouragement, he worships the Lord (Jgs 7:15; cf. 6:24).

Divided into three companies, Gid’on’s army stations itself at night outside the Midyanite stronghold. At Gid’on’s signal each man blows a trumpet (made from an animal’s horn) and smashes an empty jar containing a torch, shouting, “A sword for Yahweh and for Gid’on!” (Jgs 7:20). The effect of the clamor is overwhelming. Thinking themselves outnumbered, the confused and disheartened Midyanites flee eastward across the Yarden/Jordan. In hot pursuit, Gid’on’s men are joined by Israelis from Naftali/Naphtali, Asher, and Menasheh, who follow the enemy into the Transjordan area. The men of Efrayim/Ephraim, whose efforts are now called upon for the first time, capture and kill two of the Midyanite leaders. Angry with Gid’on for failing to enlist their services earlier, the Efrayimim/Ephraimites are nonetheless appeased by Gid’on’s tactful response to their queries (8:1-3).

Gid’on’s unselfishness shines in response to the people’s desire to make him king, but he declines (Jgs 8:22-23). He does, however, receive an immense personal fortune from the spoils of war (vv 24-26). The unfortunate conclusion of Gid’on’s story relates to his making an ephod from the gold won in battle. Perhaps a garment patterned after the high priest’s or a freestanding image, the object ensnares the people, and they worship it at Ofrah (v 27). In 2 Samuel 11:21 Gid’on’s alternate name, Yeruba’al, becomes Yerubeshet/Jerubbesheth, “Ba’al” being replaced with the Hebrew word for “shame” (besheth).

Gid’on has been singled out in the Letter to the Hebrews as a hero of the faith whose trust in God brought glory to the Lord (Heb 11:32, kjv “Gedeon”). As far back as the time of Yeshayah/Isaiah, “the day of Midyan/Midian” had become proverbial for deliverance accomplished by the hand of God apart from human strength (Is 9:4).
See also Judges, Book of.
GIDEONI

Avidan’s/Abidan’s father and leader of Benyamin’s/Benjamin’s tribe when the Israelis/Israelites were roaming in the Sinay/Sinai wilderness after their escape from Mitsrayim/Egypt (Nm 1:11; 2:22; 10:24). As leader, Gid’oni/Gideoni presented his tribe’s offering at the consecration of the tabernacle (7:60-65).
GIDOM
Place to which the Benyamite/Benjamite army was driven during a civil war between Benyamin/Benjamin and the rest of Yisrael/Israel (Jgs 20:45).
GIER EAGLE*
KJV translation for carrion vulture in Leviticus 11:18 and Deuteronomy 14:17. See Birds (Vulture, Egyptian).
GIFTS, Spiritual
See Spiritual Gifts.
GIHON, Spring of

Site in Yerushalem/Jerusalem where Shelomoh/Solomon was anointed as king (1 Kgs 1:33, 38, 45). There are two sources of running water in Yerushalem: The first is the Ayin/Ain Umm el Daraj’ (also known as the spring of the Mother of Steps, in the OT as Gihon, and to Christians as the Virgin’s Fountain), which lies at the eastern ridge. The second is Bir ’Ayub, or the well of Iyov/Job. The importance of the spring of Gihon for the defense of Yerushalem in time of siege is emphasized by Hizkiyah’s/Hezekiah’s measures to deny his enemies access to the water supply and provide access for those who defended the city (2 Kgs 20:20; 2 Chr 32:30; cf. 2 Kgs 25:4; 2 Chr 32:3-4; Is 7:3). Hizkiyah’s tunnel brought the waters from the spring of Gihon in the Kidron Valley (eastern) into the central valley where the present-day pool of Siloam is located. The spring was unable to supply all of Yerushalem’s needs after the exile, and in the Roman period aqueducts were built to bring additional water.
See also Siloam, Pool of.
GILALAI
Musician present at the dedication of the Yerushalem/Jerusalem wall, rebuilt during Ezra’s time (Neh 12:36).
GILBOA, Mount

Mountain on the east side of the plain of Yizre’el/Esdraelon between Galil/Galilee on the north and Shomron/Samaria on the south (modern Jebel Fuqu’ah). Mt Gilboa towers over the valley of Yizre’el. It is a weathered limestone ridge reaching to a height of 1,700 feet (518.1 meters) above sea level.

Many battles were fought in the area, including Deborah’s defeat of Sisera. At that time the flooding of the Kishon, which rose in Gilboa, greatly helped in the victory (Jgs 5:21). This region was the probable location of Gid’on’s/Gideon’s camp when he attacked the Midyanites/Midianites (6:33). Gilboa is mentioned by name only in connection with Sha’ul’s/Saul’s defense of the area against the Pelishtim/Philistines. Here his sons were killed, and here he himself committed suicide (1 Sm 31:1, 8; 2 Sm 1:6, 21; 21:12; 1 Chr 10:1, 8).
See also Saul #2.
GILEAD (Person)
1. Makir’s son from Menasheh’s/Manasseh’s tribe (Nm 26:29-33) and head of the clan of his descendants (26:29; 27:1) during the time of Mosheh/Moses (36:1).
2. Father of Yiftah/Jephthah during the period of the judges (Jgs 11:1-2). Yiftah was the head of the Giladim/Gileadites and judge over Yisrael/Israel.
3. Mika’el’s/Michael’s son from Gad’s tribe, who lived in Bashan during the initial settlement of Palestine (1 Chr 5:14).
GILEAD (Place)

1. Region east of the Yarden/Jordan River. Generally used to designate the territory occupied by all the Transjordanian Israeli/Israelite tribes (Jgs 20:1; 2 Kgs 10:33; Jer 50:19; Zec 10:10). Specifically, Gilead is the area of the Transjordan lying between the Yarmuk and Arnon Rivers and divided by the Yabok/Jabbok River.

The so-called Dome of Gilead is an extension of the central hill country of Yehudah/Judah, rising to heights of more than 3,000 feet (914.4 meters) above the Yarden Valley. The valleys and hills were well watered by numerous rivers and tributaries, making flatter portions of the countryside well suited for agriculture, especially olive trees, grapevines, and grains (cf. Jer 8:22; 46:11; Hos 2:8). The densely forested and rugged hills were sometimes compared to those of Levanon/Lebanon (Jer 22:6; Zec 10:10) and made the land a refuge for those in flight, since the terrain prohibited ready pursuit by enemies (cf. Gn 31:21; 1 Sm 13:7).

Originally the region of Gilead was allotted to the tribes of Re’uven/Reuben, Gad, and Menasheh/Manasseh (Nm 32). The period of the judges saw Israeli security there assailed by the Midyanites/Midianites and Amalekim/Amalekites, only to be checked by the military exploits of Gid’on/Gideon (Jgs 6–7). Half a century later, Yiftah/Jephthah was recalled from his banishment to rescue Gilead from oppressive Amoni/Ammonite rule (chs 10–11). During the united monarchy, Sha’ul/Saul delivered Yavesh-Gilead/Jabesh-gilead from Amoni dominance (1 Sm 11:1-11; 31:8-13; 2 Sm 2:1-7). Avner/Abner installed Ish-Boshet/Ish-bosheth as a rival to David in Gilead (2 Sm 2:8-9). David conquered the Amonim/Ammonites controlling Gilead as he extended the borders of Yisrael/Israel (8:11-12; 10:1-19). He fled there for refuge in the face of Avshalom’s/Absalom’s rebellion (chs 15–17) and was finally restored to the throne when Avshalom was slain in the forest of Efrayim/Ephraim (chs 18–19). Gilead remained a battleground during the divided monarchy, as first the Israelis/Israelites warred with the Aramim/Syrians (Arameans; 1 Kgs 20:23-43; 22:1-4, 29-40; 2 Kgs 13:22; Am 1:3) and then with the Assyrians, who wrested the territory from Pekah in 733 BC and deported the Israeli population, thus severing Gilead’s tie to the northern kingdom (2 Kgs 15:27-31).

2. A city condemned for its evil (Hos 6:8), possibly an abbreviated name for Yavesh-Gilead or Ramot-Gilead/Ramoth-gilead. This may be the same Gilead that was identified with Mitspah/Mizpah #5. (cf. Jgs 10:17-18).
GILEAD*, Balm of

Substance of uncertain identification and one of several resins used in the Near East for medicinal purposes. It did not grow in Gilead, but it may have received its name from being exported to Mitsrayim/Egypt and Foinikai/Phoenicia from Gilead (Gn 37:25; Ez 27:17). The substance supposedly had astringent, antiseptic, and other therapeutic qualities.
See also Medicine and Medical Practice; Plants (Balm).
GILEADITE
Name given to Israelis/Israelites from the two and a half Transjordanian tribes. See Gilead (Place) #1; Gilead (Person) #1, #2.
GILGAL

1. Town near Yeriho/Jericho. Gilgal was assigned to Benyamin’s/Benjamin’s tribe when Kena’an/Canaan was divided among the tribes of Yisrael/Israel. For many years it was a center of religious, political, and military importance, especially during the periods of the conquest of Kena’an and the early monarchy under Sha’ul/Saul.

Gilgal was the first place where Yisrael encamped in Palestine after the miraculous crossing of the Yarden/Jordan River (Jos 4:19). No doubt the tabernacle was set up here, since Yisrael occupied Gilgal for some time and used it as the center of the commonwealth. Several significant religious events occurred at Gilgal: the circumcision of all Hebrew males born in the wilderness during the 40 years of wandering (5:2-9), the celebration of the Passover (v 10), the cessation of the manna (v 12), and a divine manifestation to Yehoshua/Joshua by the “commander of the army of Yahweh” (vv 13-15).

Militarily, Gilgal was Yisrael’s first foothold in Kena’an and the base of operations for the Conquest. From here Yehoshua led Yisrael to the conquest of Yeriho (Jos 6) and Ay/Ai (8:3), formed a treaty with the Givonim/Gibeonites (9:3-15), attacked the five Amori/Amorite kings (10:6-43), and launched his northern campaign (ch 11). At Gilgal, Yehudah/Judah, Menasheh/Manasseh, and Efrayim/Ephraim were assigned their portions of Palestine (chs 15–17).

After the relocation of the tabernacle at Shiloh, Gilgal retained its importance to Yisrael. It was one of the towns visited regularly by Shmuel/Samuel in his annual circuit as judge (1 Sm 7:16) and was one of the primary places for offering sacrifices (10:8; 13:9-10; 15:21). At Gilgal, Sha’ul, a Benyamite/Benjamite, was crowned king (11:14-15), and later rejected (13:4-15; 15:17-31). Here the men of Yehudah met David returning to Palestine after Avshalom’s/Absalom’s rebellion (2 Sm 19:15). That Gilgal was still a religious center of some importance as late as the eighth century BC is indicated in the denunciation by Hoshea/Hosea and Amos of the sanctuary and sacrificial cult located there (Hos 4:15; 9:15; 12:11; Am 4:4; 5:5).

The exact location of Gilgal is disputed among archaeologists. Some locate it at Khirbet en-Nitleh about two miles (3.2 kilometers) east of modern Yeriho. Others prefer Khirbet Mefjir, a mound about one mile (1.6 kilometers) from ancient Yeriho (Tell es-Sultan). Joshua 4:19 places it on the eastern border of Yeriho, and Josephus gives the distance from the Yarden fording place to Gilgal as 50 stadia (5.8 miles, or 9.3 kilometers), with Gilgal being about 10 stadia from Yeriho (Antiquities 5.6.4). These distances fit best with Khirbet Mefjir.
2. Place perhaps near Yeriho (Dt 11:30); however, the language of the passage implies that it is located in the neighborhood of Mt Eyval/Ebal and Mt Gerizim.
3. KJV rendering of “Goiim in Galilee” in Joshua 12:23. Although its location is uncertain, the context places it in northern Palestine in the area of Galil/Galilee. See Goiim #2.
4. Place describing the northern border of Yehudah (Jos 15:7). It was near Adumim/Adummim and was perhaps identifiable with Gelilot/Geliloth in Joshua 18:17.

5. Place mentioned in connection with Eliyah/Elijah and Elisha (2 Kgs 2:1; 4:38). It was apparently a town farther from the Yarden River than #1 above. In the story of Eliyah’s translation into heaven, he and Elisha were going from Gilgal to Beyt-El/Bethel to Yeriho. Since the account places Beyt-El between Gilgal and Yeriho, it could not have been the first Gilgal. It may refer to the modern Jiljiliah, a town on top of a hill in central Palestine, about seven miles (11.3 kilometers) north of Beyt-El.
GILGAMESH EPIC*

Popular legendary composition about a Sumerian hero’s life of adventure and acquisition of wisdom. Gilgamesh was king of Uruk, or Erek/Erech (Tell Obeid; modern Warka), at the end of the fourth millennium BC. The legend, which emerged from the first Babylonian dynasty (about 1830–1530 BC), was discovered in the palace library of Ashurbanipal (669–627 BC) at Nineveh.

Written on 12 tablets, the Gilgamesh Epic tells how a strong ruler, Gilgamesh, became friends with Enkidu, a hunter the gods had created to overthrow him. Together the two killed the monster Huwawa. Ishtar, the goddess of love, made advances to Gilgamesh. In resisting her, he killed the sacred heavenly bull. Enkidu died as a punishment for that crime. Gilgamesh, overcome by grief, traveled the world seeking the source of immortality, finally arriving at the homeland of Utnapishtim. In Tablet XI Utnapishtim describes a devastating flood that drowned a large area of Mesopotamia. Through his piety Utnapishtim was saved and given immortality by the gods. The final tablet contains an expression of sadness over Gilgamesh’s mortality.

Biblical scholars have compared the epic’s flood narrative with the one in the book of Genesis. Both accounts concern a flood, a person or persons to be delivered, the sending out of birds, and a sacrifice made by the hero. There are, however, several differences. The biblical account gives a moral reason for the Flood; the Gilgamesh Epic has a more frivolous one: the gods were irritated by human noise. The types of birds, names of heroes, dimensions of the ark, and duration of the flood all differ. The Genesis account clearly does not depend on the epic. Both may go back to a common tradition. It is also possible that the two accounts are independent descriptions of the same devastating flood.
See also Flood, The; Noah #1.
GILO*, GILOH, GILONITE*

Village, and the inhabitants, in the mountains of southern Yehudah/Judah (Jos 15:51). David’s counselor Ahitofel/Ahithophel was a Giloni/Gilonite (2 Sm 15:12; 23:34). It has been identified with modern Khirbet Jala just northeast of Hevron/Hebron.
GIMZO
Town of Yehudah/Judah captured by the Pelishtim/Philistines during King Ahaz’s reign (2 Chr 28:18). It is modern Jimzu, located southeast of Ludd (Lod/Lydda).
GINATH
Tivni’s/Tibni’s father. Tivni unsuccessfully attempted to gain the throne of Yisrael/Israel; Omri became king instead (1 Kgs 16:21-22).
GINNETHON

2. Priest and head of Meshulam’s/Meshullam’s household during the postexilic days of Yoyakim/Joiakim the high priest (Neh 12:16).
GIRDLE*

GIRGASHITES

Kena’ani/Canaanite tribe (Gn 10:16; 1 Chr 1:14) whose land was promised to Avraham/Abraham (Gn 15:21; Dt 7:1; Jos 3:10) and was ultimately acquired (Jos 24:11; Neh 9:8). The tribe’s location is unknown, though they may have lived in Karkisha, a city mentioned in Hiti/Hittite texts, or in Kirkishati, an area east of the Hidekel/Tigris. The name Gresh appeared in 13th century BC Ugaritic texts and might indicate a tribe. In Matthew 8:28; Mark 5:1; and Luke 8:26, a name variously translated as “Gergesenes” (kjv), “Gerasainon/Gerasenes,” and “Gadarainos/Gadarenes” may preserve the tradition of Girgashi/Girgashite occupation of Palestine.
GIRZITES

The Hebrew text has girzi, while the marginal variant transposes two consonants to read gizri, “Gezrites.” The Greek version follows the Hebrew marginal variant. The confusion of the name is obviously early. If “Gerzites” is the original, they could have been a Kena’ani/Canaanite tribe living in the Mt Gerizim area. GISHPA, GISPA*
Overseer of the temple servants in Nehemyah’s/Nehemiah’s time (Neh 11:21, kjv “Gispa”); perhaps alternately called Hasufa/Hasupha in Ezra 2:43 and Nehemiah 7:46. See Hasupha.
GITTAH-HEPHER*
KJV form of the town Gat-Hahefer/Gath-hepher, in Joshua 19:13. See Gath-hepher.
GITTAIM

GITTITE

GITTITH*

Obscure Hebrew term in the superscriptions of Psalms 8, 81, and 84 (nlt mg); perhaps a musical instrument or a musical cue, signaling a mood, to which the psalms were to be performed. See Music; Musical Instruments.
GIZON, GIZONITE*

Designation for Hashem (Yashen/Jashen, nlt), one of David’s mighty men (1 Chr 11:34). Gizon may have been an ancient Kena’ani/Canaanite settlement. Some scholars have emended the text to read “Guni/Gunite” (cf. 1 Chr 5:15; 7:13) or “from Gimzo” (cf. 2 Chr 28:18).
GLASS
Translation for “mirror” in Isaiah 3:23, 1 Corinthians 13:12, and James 1:23 (kjv). Since mirrors of Bible times were polished metal sheets, “glass” is incorrect. See Mirror.
GLEAN, GLEANING

Practice of allowing the poor to follow reapers in a field to pick up missed spears of grain (cf. Lv 19:9; 23:22; Dt 24:19; Ru 2:2-23).
